newCards.title: The Moved Fence Posts
newCards.flavor: Before dawn you find a man resetting four fence posts three rows deep into his neighbor's orchard, so that a small seep spring falls on his side of the line. His two children follow with buckets and say nothing. His own well went dry in spring. He sees you watching, straightens, and asks you to keep walking.

choices.label: Wake the orchard family
choices.intent: Knock at the neighbor's door and tell them plainly what is happening to their line.
choices.risk: If you tell the truth, his children face another dry week.

success.text: You wake the orchard family with the shovel still in the earth. The stolen posts are pulled before breakfast, and the spring stays on the old boundary. The man leads his children home with their buckets empty. Nobody thanks you for telling the truth; nobody disputes that it needed telling.

choices.label: Broker a share of the spring
choices.intent: Bring both households to the seep and argue for alternate days of water.
choices.risk: One spring, two families, and neither trusts a stranger to divide it.

success.text: It takes the whole morning and two shouting matches, but they agree: his buckets at dawn, hers at dusk. The neighbor's wife hands you a wedge of cornbread, and the man nods once, which is more than you expected.

failure.text: Old grievances come up faster than water. The neighbor shoves the man, the man shoves you, and you go down hard against a post. The line stays where he set it, for now.

choices.label: Help him tamp the posts
choices.intent: Lend your back to his work before the orchard family wakes, and share his breakfast.
choices.risk: If the neighbors catch you, you are part of the theft.

success.text: The posts go in firm and straight. His children fill their buckets at the seep, and he pays you in dried beans and silence. Up the hill, a lamp is lit in the orchard house.

failure.text: The neighbor's dog finds you first. You take a bite across the forearm getting clear of it, and the man leaves you to explain the shovel in your hands.

choices.label: Make him pull them out
choices.intent: Stand close and let him see you have hurt people before, until he undoes it.
choices.risk: Frightened men holding shovels do not always back down.

success.text: He looks at your hands and then at his children, and pulls every post himself. The spring stays with the orchard. His youngest watches you the whole time with flat, frightened eyes.

failure.text: He swings the shovel before he thinks. The flat of it catches your shoulder, and by the time you are up, his children are crying and the posts are still standing.

newCards.title: The Collector's Ledger
newCards.flavor: The collector sits on a farmhouse step with an open ledger across his knees. Three sacks of seed corn stand beside the door: the family's next crop, if the office does not take them today. He is painfully polite. Ride home with fewer than three, he says, and a crueller clerk takes his place. The farmer's wife keeps one hand on the nearest sack.

choices.label: Pay part from your pack
choices.intent: Set your own food down against the debt, so the family keeps enough seed to plant.
choices.risk: Your food can save one sack of seed corn, but not feed you tomorrow.

success.text: The collector weighs your food in his hands, writes it down carefully, and leaves one sack behind. The family keeps enough seed to plant. They have nothing to give you, and they are too ashamed to say so.

choices.label: Check his sums
choices.intent: Ask to read the ledger and look for the place where the numbers do not hold.
choices.risk: If the figures are honest, you have spent the family's last chance to bargain.

success.text: The interest has been figured twice, once in ink and once in pencil. He goes red, corrects it, and leaves with one sack instead of three. The wife wraps a cold potato and a heel of bread for you.

failure.text: Every sum adds up. The collector closes his ledger with a care that feels like a reprimand, then loads all three sacks. The wife does not blame you aloud. She looks past you at the bare place where next spring's planting stood.

choices.label: Ask what he fears
choices.intent: Talk to the man under the clerk, and learn what he would risk to ride home lighter.
choices.risk: Pity can harden when it is named out loud.

success.text: He admits the new office manager counts sacks, not farms. Together you write the place down as abandoned, and he rides off with nothing and a lie he will have to carry. The family promises to remember you.

failure.text: He hears pity and takes it as contempt. He loads all three sacks, writes your description in the margin of his ledger, and warns the family not to shelter you again.

choices.label: Help him load the sacks
choices.intent: Carry the sacks to his mule, since the debt is real and the law is his.
choices.risk: The family will remember whose hands carried their seed.

success.text: He thanks you and pours a cup of corn into your pack for the trouble. The wife does not shut the door when you leave. She stands in it and watches you all the way to the road.

newCards.title: The Three-Wheeled Wagon
newCards.flavor: A wagon with three wheels lies tilted against the border fence, the fourth in pieces in the ditch. Two parents and a grandmother sit in its shade with their children, a long way from wherever they started. The farmer at the gate holds a rifle and says the last band of travelers stripped his trees bare. He wants them gone by sundown.

choices.label: Speak for the family
choices.intent: Ask the farmer for one night in his barn, and stand surety for their honesty.
choices.risk: If the travelers steal one apple, the farmer will come looking for you.

success.text: The farmer lowers the rifle a hand's width at a time. They get the barn, and you get the hayloft above them. At dawn every apple is still on the trees, and he almost smiles as he hands you two of them.

failure.text: He hears a stranger taking their side and orders all of you off. You walk the family to the ditch line and sleep beside them on hard ground, and wake stiff and cold.

choices.label: Lash a skid to the axle
choices.intent: Cut a fence rail into a skid so the wagon can drag on before sundown.
choices.risk: The only sound fence rail belongs to the man holding the rifle.

success.text: The skid holds, scraping a long groove into the road as the wagon lurches away. The grandmother presses a small jar of honey into your hands. Behind you, the farmer counts his fence rails and swears.

failure.text: The rail splits under the load and a splinter goes deep into your palm. The family thanks you anyway, and the farmer holds up the broken rail as proof of everything he said.

choices.label: Give them your food
choices.intent: Hand your provisions to the parents so they need nothing from his trees tonight.
choices.risk: You walk on lighter, with nothing given back.

success.text: You give the parents your last provisions. They count portions for the children before either adult touches a crumb. From the gate the farmer watches, his rifle suddenly an awkward thing to hold. He goes inside without a word. You leave hungry, with a small child's wave following you down the road.

choices.label: Guide them by the drove road
choices.intent: Lead the wagon onto the old cattle track that skirts the farms entirely.
choices.risk: The old track is rough, and it adds a long day.

success.text: You find the drove road where the grass grows a different green and walk the family down it. The way ahead now bends through hills you had not meant to cross, but no gate along it has a rifle.

failure.text: The track has washed out at the first creek. You haul the wagon across by hand until your back gives, then lead them back to the farmer's road, sore and no closer.

newCards.title: A Tithe Basket at the Gate
newCards.flavor: An empty wicker basket sits at the farm gate between two road wardens and three hungry raccoon children. The wardens say protection is payable in apples: their wages stopped in spring. The younger one keeps a club ready. The older woman has not eaten either, if her hollow cheeks tell the truth. Neither looks at the orchard when she says what they will take.

choices.label: Stand at the gate
choices.intent: Put yourself between the wardens and the orchard and tell them to ride on.
choices.risk: Wardens remember faces, and they carry clubs.

success.text: You stand there long enough that the younger warden loses his nerve. They leave with an empty basket and a long look at you. The family's apples stay in their cellar, and your face stays in the wardens' memory.

failure.text: The club takes you across the ribs, then again. When you can stand, the basket is full and gone. The mother helps you up, and the wardens have your face now.

choices.label: Fill the basket yourself
choices.intent: Empty your own pack into the basket so the family keeps their winter apples.
choices.risk: You can buy the family's winter apples at the cost of your own next meals.

success.text: You empty your provisions into the basket. The older warden weighs them with her eyes, then waves her companion back to the road. Behind the fence, the children have kept their apples. You take the next mile with an empty pack; at the gate, nobody is sure whom to thank.

choices.label: Bargain with the older warden
choices.intent: Ask what her own family needs, and offer a half basket she can defend.
choices.risk: An offer she cannot defend to her captain may cost her the post.

success.text: She has three children in a garrison town and no letters from her captain. She takes half, warns you which road her riders sweep tomorrow, and says she owes you one for the arithmetic. The way ahead changes.

failure.text: She hears a stranger telling her how to do her job. The basket goes out full, and she asks your name twice, as if she means to remember it.

choices.label: Claim their captain sent you
choices.intent: Since the wardens know your face already, let them believe you came to inspect them.
choices.risk: If the bluff breaks, they settle an old grudge.

success.text: They already know your face, and that does half the work. The younger one goes pale, and they leave the basket and ride. The family stares at you as if you might be dangerous after all.

failure.text: The older warden laughs. Their captain, she says, does not hire strangers. You pay for the bluff with a beating, and the basket fills while you are still in the ditch.

newCards.title: The Noon Water Line
newCards.flavor: At noon the line for the well runs past the trough and out into the full sun. A man with a sick ox shoves toward the front, saying the animal will die before his turn. Behind you, a young mother rocks a baby whose lips are cracked. The keeper rations every cup and says the water will not last the line.

choices.label: Give the mother your place
choices.intent: Step out of line and send the mother forward to drink in your place.
choices.risk: The last cup may be drawn before you reach the well again.

success.text: She drinks and wets the baby's lips before she thanks you. By the time the line comes round again the bucket scrapes stone, and you walk on with your mouth dry and your head pounding.

choices.label: Look at the ox yourself
choices.intent: Read the ox and the man, and decide whether he is lying about the dying.
choices.risk: If you are wrong, the mother or the ox will go without.

success.text: The ox's tongue is black and swollen; the man is telling the truth. You talk the line into one bucket for the animal, and later he gives you a strip of dried meat from his saddlebag.

failure.text: You say the ox can wait. An hour later it folds onto its knees and stays there, its tongue black against the dust. The man crouches beside its neck, silent. The mother drinks; the line shuffles forward around the pair of them.

choices.label: Hold him back by force
choices.intent: Block the man's way so the line keeps its order and the mother keeps her turn.
choices.risk: A desperate man fights harder than he looks.

success.text: He comes at you once and you put him on the ground. The line holds and the mother drinks. The man drags his ox into the shade and does not look at anyone again.

failure.text: He is stronger than his thirst made him look. His elbow catches your jaw, and while you are down he pushes through to the bucket and drinks first.

choices.label: Follow the wet stones
choices.intent: Trace a dark stain under the trough to wherever the water is being lost.
choices.risk: You could lose your place for nothing.

success.text: A cracked stone in the channel has been leaking half of every bucket into the sand. You pack it with clay, and the water stretches far enough for everyone. The keeper fills your flask without counting.

failure.text: The stain leads nowhere but under the stones. When you come back your place is gone, and you wait out the afternoon at the back of the line in the full sun, dizzy with heat.

newCards.title: The Dowser's Hazel Fork
newCards.flavor: A dowser paces dry ground beyond the well, a fork of hazel trembling in his hands. Three families follow him carrying spades, each already a coin poorer. Wherever the fork bends he plants a stone and asks for another coin before anyone digs. The toes of his boots have split open. He watches the children's faces when he names his price.

choices.label: Watch his hands closely
choices.intent: Follow the fork and his wrists to see whether the wood moves or he does.
choices.risk: If you expose him, the families lose both their water and their last hope.

success.text: His thumbs turn the fork; the dip is his. You tell the families, and he does not deny it. He gives their coins back, then sits in the dust and says his own children have not eaten in two days.

failure.text: You call him a cheat, and the fork dips again in front of everyone. The families close ranks around him and send you back to the well with your accusation still in your mouth.

choices.label: Walk the ground with him
choices.intent: Read the plants and the lay of the land, and test whether there is water at all.
choices.risk: A day of digging in the sun, maybe for nothing.

success.text: Where deep-rooted mesquite grows in a line, an old water seam runs under the hill. You dig together and strike damp clay by evening. The families press a bag of meal on you, and the road ahead now bends to meet their new well.

failure.text: You dig where the plants say water should be and find only rock. By sundown your hands are raw and your back burns, and the dowser looks almost relieved that you failed too.

choices.label: Take his coin and keep quiet
choices.intent: Accept the share he offers you to say nothing about how the fork moves.
choices.risk: Your silence will send three families digging where he knows the earth is dry.

success.text: He slips you a coin and a twist of jerky while the families gather their tools. Behind you, spades strike dry earth in a hopeful rhythm. At the bend in the road you can still hear them singing. The next mile is quiet enough to count your payment twice.

newCards.title: A Padlock on the Well Lid
newCards.flavor: Someone has fitted an iron lid over the well and closed it with a heavy padlock. The keeper's grown son sits beside it, selling water by the cup. He says the level drops a hand each week, and if everyone drank freely there would be none by harvest. A family with a dry cart stands waiting, with nothing left to trade.

choices.label: Pay for two cups
choices.intent: Pay the son's price for your cup and one more for the waiting family.
choices.risk: Your ration buys theirs, while the lock remains on a public well.

success.text: He takes your food and pours two cups exactly to the line. The family drinks slowly, making it last, and so do you. The son checks the level afterward, and you cannot tell whether he is greedy or afraid.

choices.label: Pick the lock at night
choices.intent: Come back after dark, open the lid, and fill the family's barrels while he sleeps.
choices.risk: He sleeps lightly, and he keeps a cudgel.

success.text: The lock gives on the third try. You fill the family's barrels and your own flask, then lock it again behind you. In the morning the son measures the level, and his face goes gray.

failure.text: The lock clatters against the lid. He is on you before you can run, and the cudgel finds your back twice before you get clear of the yard.

choices.label: Measure the water with him
choices.intent: Help him sound the well and work out a ration that is fair to everyone.
choices.risk: If the numbers are bad, nobody gets what they hoped.

success.text: The water is lower than he said, but steady. You chalk a line on the stones and a ration beside it, two cups a household a day. He unlocks the lid for the family and asks you to stand witness when the neighbors come.

failure.text: The weighted line catches and you lose your footing on the wet rim, wrenching your knee. The son helps you up, but he locks the lid again before he does.

choices.label: Break the lid open
choices.intent: Smash the padlock off so no one has to buy water from a public well.
choices.risk: You can break a lock, but not fill a well after the rush of buckets.

success.text: The hasp tears away. The waiting family fills its cart and a dozen others come running, cups held out like claims. The keeper's son says nothing as he lowers the measuring line. He lets you see how little wet rope comes back. Everyone has water today. He asks whose name to give the families who arrive tomorrow.

failure.text: The iron holds, and the shock of the blow runs up both arms. The son does not even stand. The family turns their cart back toward the road, still thirsty.

newCards.title: A Ribbon on the Windlass
newCards.flavor: A faded blue ribbon is knotted tight around the well's windlass handle. A woman sits on the rim beside it and tells you her daughter tied it there the morning she walked to the refuge for bread. The sisters sent word that the girl was placed on a farm in the east. No letter has come, and the ribbon is starting to fray.

choices.label: Tell her what you suspect
choices.intent: Tell her honestly that the refuge's stories do not match, and that she should ask hard questions.
choices.risk: She may go looking for her daughter alone, with nothing stronger than your suspicion.

success.text: She listens without interrupting. Then she unties the ribbon, winds it around her wrist, and starts down the refuge road before you can offer to walk with her. You do not know whether you helped.

choices.label: Tell her the farm is real
choices.intent: Tell her placements like that are common, so she can sleep tonight.
choices.risk: A reassuring lie may cost her the days she has left to search.

success.text: You tell her the east is full of farms taking apprentices. Her shoulders finally loosen. She leaves the ribbon tied for her daughter to find and walks home. At the well you draw a full bucket; halfway through drinking you remember how little you actually know.

choices.label: Search the ground for signs
choices.intent: Look around the well for anything the girl left on the morning she went.
choices.risk: Old tracks can lie, and so can hope.

success.text: Under the trough you find a pebble tally scratched into the stone, with an arrow toward the refuge road. The mother says her daughter counted days that way. You follow the arrow with your eyes, and the road ahead no longer looks the same.

failure.text: You crawl the well-head until your knees are raw and find only cart ruts and old cups. The mother thanks you for trying in a voice that has stopped expecting anything.

choices.label: Carry her water home
choices.intent: Walk her home with full buckets and listen to everything she remembers.
choices.risk: It is a long walk in heat you cannot spare.

success.text: You set the buckets down in a kitchen with two places laid and one unused. She talks the whole way, and you learn the girl was not the first child from these farms placed in the east. She sends you off with flatbread.

failure.text: The yoke raises a blister across your shoulders before the second mile. You deliver every drop, but you arrive spent, and she has to give you a cup from the bucket you carried.

newCards.title: Bread Under the Long Table
newCards.flavor: One long table, twelve counted loaves, and a sister who watches the bread instead of the children. Beside you, a hungry boy hides a crust under the table for later. Her eyes follow his hand. Above the door hangs the mission rule: anyone caught stealing sleeps outside the walls, family included. His mother has already begun folding the blankets at her feet.

choices.label: Say the bread was yours
choices.intent: Tell the sister you passed the boy your own share, and take the rule on yourself.
choices.risk: You can keep the boy's family indoors by accepting punishment yourself.

success.text: The sister's mouth tightens, but she cannot call you a thief for giving away your own bread. She walks you to the gate anyway. The boy's family stays inside, and the dust blows all night against your back.

choices.label: Plead for the boy
choices.intent: Ask the sister quietly whether a hungry child is what the rule was made for.
choices.risk: Questioning the rule at supper marks you as trouble.

success.text: She looks at the boy for a long moment and lets it go. Later, clearing plates, she says the Abbess counts the bread herself every night, and that a missing loaf is never forgiven twice. She slips a spare heel into your pack.

failure.text: She calls a senior sister, and the boy's family is sent out into the dust before the plates are cleared. You did not save them, and now every sister at the table knows your face.

choices.label: Point out the boy
choices.intent: Tell the sister what you saw, since the rule exists to feed everyone fairly.
choices.risk: The sisters may praise your honesty while they send his family into the night.

success.text: You point to the boy. The sister takes back the bread, then presses the confiscated crust into your hand as payment for keeping order. The family gathers its blankets and goes outside. The bread is still warm. The boy's mother keeps her eyes on the door rather than on you.

choices.label: Slip the bread back unseen
choices.intent: Lift the loaf from the boy's shirt and return it to the basket before the count.
choices.risk: You could be caught with stolen bread in hand.

success.text: Your hand moves while the sister turns to pour. The loaf is back in the basket, the count comes out right, and the boy stares at you as if you robbed him, which you did.

failure.text: The sister turns back too soon and finds the loaf in your hand. You are walked to the gate as the thief and spend a cold night outside the wall, and the boy keeps his bread.

newCards.title: The Refuge Lantern at Midnight
newCards.flavor: The old sister who tends the refuge lantern asks you to keep it burning while she sleeps an hour, so travelers can find the walls through the dust. Near midnight, a covered cart rolls out through the back gate without a light of its own. Under its canvas something small shifts, and the lantern beside you needs oil.

choices.label: Keep the lantern burning
choices.intent: Stay at your post and keep the light alive, as you promised the old sister.
choices.risk: Travelers will find shelter, but the unlit cart will pass without a witness.

success.text: You trim the wick and spend the last of the oil watching for shapes on the road. Two travelers arrive before dawn, following your light with their hands held out. The covered cart never returns. When the old sister thanks you, she notices the empty oil tin but does not ask where you were looking all night.

choices.label: Follow the cart in the dark
choices.intent: Leave the lantern and trail the cart's tracks as far as the night allows.
choices.risk: Every minute you follow the cart is a minute the lost cannot see the gate.

success.text: The cart takes an unmarked track east into the hills, toward a ridge you have never seen on any map. You turn back at the first rise. The road ahead is not the one you thought it was.

failure.text: You lose the cart in the dust within a mile and stumble back bruised from a fall. The lantern has burned out, and at dawn a lost traveler is found huddled against the outer wall, alive and frightened.

choices.label: Wake the old sister
choices.intent: Wake her gently and ask where carts go at midnight without a light.
choices.risk: She may be loyal to the house before the truth.

success.text: She watches the dark where the cart went and says they are farm placements, as they always are. Then, quieter, she says she has kept the lantern for eleven years and never seen a letter come back.

failure.text: She says you dreamed it and takes back the lantern. By morning a senior sister knows you were asking about carts, and your breakfast is set at the far end of the table, away from everyone.

newCards.title: The Guest Book on the Lectern
newCards.flavor: Inside the refuge door, a thick guest book lies open on a carved lectern. A cheerful secretary dips a pen and asks you to sign, as every traveler does. On the open page, families have written their children's names beside their own. Each child's name has a line for departure, and few of those lines are filled.

choices.label: Read the earlier pages
choices.intent: Turn back through the months while you pretend to search for a friend's name.
choices.risk: If she catches you reading the missing departures, she will mark your own arrival.

success.text: Month after month, the children's departure lines stay blank, and in places the paper has been scraped thin with a knife. You close the book, sign a plain name, and keep your hand steady.

failure.text: The secretary turns the book back to today's page with one finger and keeps it there. Her smile does not change, but she writes something small in the margin beside your name.

choices.label: Tear out a page
choices.intent: Wait for the secretary to turn away, then take one page as proof.
choices.risk: A stolen page is proof only if you can carry it out unseen.

success.text: The page comes away with a dry whisper. Between your shirts you hide a list of children who entered the refuge and a blank column where their departures should be. You have stolen a record, not rescued a child. For the first time, you know where to start asking.

failure.text: The tear is louder than you expected. You are walked out into the dust with a sister on each arm, gripped hard enough to bruise, and the book is locked away behind you.

choices.label: Sign and ask outright
choices.intent: Sign your name and ask the secretary plainly why so many lines are empty.
choices.risk: A plain question gets a practiced answer, or worse.

success.text: She gives the practiced answer about farm placements. Then, because you keep looking at her, she gives a smaller one: the Abbess records departures in a separate book. She does not say where it is kept.

failure.text: Her smile holds and her eyes go cold. She thanks you for your concern and sends you in to supper, and you feel her watching you all the way down the corridor.

choices.label: Ask a friend to distract her
choices.intent: Someone on this road owes you; ask them to keep the secretary busy a while.
choices.risk: If they are caught, the debt runs the other way.

success.text: Someone you once helped arrives at the desk with a long, loud complaint about lost luggage. While the secretary soothes them, you read a year of empty lines. On the way out they wink and say you are even.

failure.text: Your friend's complaint is too loud and too short. The secretary sends for a sister, and you both leave with apologies and nothing to show for the favor you spent.

newCards.title: The Infirmary's Last Cot
newCards.flavor: In the refuge infirmary only the last cot is filled: a drover shivering with fever. The nursing sister has run out of willow bark, though a full store sits behind the locked door of the children's wing, kept by the Abbess's order. The sister keeps looking from the drover to that door, and her hands will not stay still.

choices.label: Give him your own medicine
choices.intent: Open your pack and spend your herbs on a stranger the house will not treat.
choices.risk: The drover gets your last medicine. The next fever will be yours to face barehanded.

success.text: You steep the herbs and hold the cup while he drinks. By dawn the fever has broken. He cannot pay, and he is gone before breakfast, leaving only a warm hollow in the cot.

choices.label: Take bark from the locked store
choices.intent: Slip into the children's wing and take what the drover needs from the store.
choices.risk: That door is locked for a reason you do not know.

success.text: The store holds blankets and medicine for twenty children. The wing beyond it holds stripped beds and no one at all. You take two twists of bark, one for the drover and one for your pack.

failure.text: A key turns behind you. You are caught in the store with your hands full and turned out before dawn, bruised by the grip of the sisters who dragged you. The drover is still burning.

choices.label: Sit up with him all night
choices.intent: Cool his face with wet cloths until morning, since there is nothing else to give.
choices.risk: You can give him a night's company, but not the willow bark he needs.

success.text: You wring wet cloths until your knuckles ache and dawn turns the window grey. The drover is breathing, though the fever has not broken. The nursing sister takes the cloth from you and says she will stay. You never learn whether he lives, only that he was not left alone.

choices.label: Ask the sister to defy orders
choices.intent: Tell the nursing sister that a rule which lets a man die is not the Abbess's to make.
choices.risk: Push too hard and she reports you, not the rule.

success.text: She goes for the key with her jaw set. When she comes back with the bark, she whispers that no child has slept in that wing for a month, and then asks you to forget she said it.

failure.text: She bursts into tears and runs to the senior sister. You are given a blanket and a seat by the outer gate for the night, where the cold gets into your bones.

newCards.title: One Too Many Aboard
newCards.flavor: You were the last to step aboard, and now the pilot counts heads twice and says her ferry carries ten, not eleven. Brown water laps at the deck boards, and a trader's three oil casks crowd the stern. An old woman with a bundle of quilts starts to rise from the bench, and her grandson holds her sleeve so tightly his knuckles go pale.

choices.label: Step back onto the landing
choices.intent: Climb off before the old woman can, and wait on the bank for tomorrow's crossing.
choices.risk: Another night on the landing eats food you cannot spare.

success.text: The ferry pulls away with ten aboard, the grandson waving until the haze takes him. You sleep under the landing's eaves and eat tomorrow's supper tonight, listening to the river go by without you.

choices.label: Heave the oil casks overboard
choices.intent: Roll the trader's casks into the river so the ferry rides high enough for everyone.
choices.risk: The trader has a knife and his whole savings aboard.

success.text: Three casks splash into the current and the deck lifts a hand's width. All eleven of you reach the far bank dry, and the trader stalks off swearing he will describe your face to every warden downriver.

failure.text: The trader throws his shoulder into you before the first cask moves, and you go down hard against the rail. While you are still catching your breath, the old woman steps off onto the landing without a word.

choices.label: Question the pilot's count
choices.intent: Ask the pilot to show everyone the load mark she measures by.
choices.risk: If she is honest, you have shamed her for nothing.

success.text: The load mark is painted a hand below where the hull truly rides; she has been selling the eleventh seat to whoever is desperate enough to pay. She lets everyone ride and does not look at you again.

failure.text: The mark is honest, and the river proves it: a swell slops over the rail and soaks every bundle on deck, your rations among them. The pilot puts you ashore to lighten the load, and the old woman keeps her seat.

newCards.title: The Smuggler's Mirror
newCards.flavor: A young woman in a ferry hand's apron presses a cracked hand mirror into your palm. Her brother is poling a raft of untaxed flour down from the hills, and someone on the bank must flash the mirror at dawn, when the toll keeper's men change watch. She says that flour feeds the whole landing, and the toll would take half of it.

choices.label: Flash the signal at dawn
choices.intent: Crouch in the reeds at first light and catch the sun in the mirror when the watch turns.
choices.risk: The toll men know every glint on this bank.

success.text: The raft slides past the empty watch post in the gray light. By noon there is flour in every pot on the landing, and the young woman leaves a warm loaf at your feet and shows you the smugglers' path, which changes your road ahead.

failure.text: You flash too early, and a watchman's lantern swings toward your reeds. The raft turns back upriver, and you run the bank with his shouts behind you, knowing he got a long look at your face.

choices.label: Sell the plan to the watch
choices.intent: Carry the mirror to the toll keeper's men and find out what the warning is worth.
choices.risk: The landing will learn who talked.

success.text: The watch captain weighs the mirror in his hand and pays you in hard biscuits. At dawn his men take the raft and the flour, and the young woman's brother sits in irons on the gate steps.

failure.text: The captain takes the mirror and your story and pays you nothing, because informers are cheap here. The young woman sees you leave his post, and by evening every door on the landing closes as you pass.

choices.label: Hand the mirror back
choices.intent: Return the mirror and tell her plainly that this is not a risk you will take.
choices.risk: She may not find anyone else before dawn.

success.text: She takes the mirror without arguing and goes looking for someone braver or hungrier. At dawn you hear shouting from the gate, and you never learn whether the raft made it through.

newCards.title: A Barge Flying Yellow
newCards.flavor: A barge rides at anchor off the landing with a yellow rag tied to its mast, the old sign for fever aboard. The landing folk keep a man with a boat hook on the dock to push it off if it drifts closer. Someone aboard has been calling for clean water since morning, and the voice is getting weaker.

choices.label: Row out with water
choices.intent: Borrow a skiff, fill every skin you carry, and row the water out to the barge yourself.
choices.risk: Fever does not care why you came.

success.text: A woman with cracked lips takes the skins over the rail and cannot find the voice to thank you. By evening your own head is pounding, and the landing folk make you sleep apart from them, out on the dock.

choices.label: Argue for a berth
choices.intent: Stand on the dock and persuade the landing folk to give the barge the far berth.
choices.risk: Frightened people hate being told they are wrong.

success.text: You tell them fever spreads faster on a crowded barge than on a guarded dock, and the river carries it to them either way. Grudgingly they allow a berth at the far end, and the sick come ashore at last.

failure.text: The man with the boat hook shoves you off the dock into the shallows, and nobody reaches down to help you out. You wade ashore bruised, the barge stays where it is, and the calling goes on.

choices.label: Board with your medicine
choices.intent: Climb aboard with the herbs you carry and sort the dying from the merely sick.
choices.risk: There are more sick aboard than herbs in your bag.

success.text: Most of them have river flux, not fever, and willow bark and boiled water will see them through. The barge captain cuts down the yellow rag herself and presses a jar of honey into your hands.

failure.text: You spend every leaf you carry and lose two of them anyway before dawn. You row back aching and hollow-eyed, with an empty herb bag and the yellow rag still hanging from the mast behind you.

choices.label: Walk away from the dock
choices.intent: Keep your distance, as the landing folk do, and see to your own crossing.
choices.risk: The calling will follow you onto the ferry.

success.text: You take the first ferry out, and from midstream you can still hear the voice from the barge, thinner now. No one on the ferry speaks of it, and neither do you.

newCards.title: The Swimmer's Purse
newCards.flavor: The ferry crews hang a leather purse of crossing tokens from the far pier for anyone who can swim the channel. A thin father has already pulled off his boots while his three children watch from the mud. The crews are laying bets on the pier, and the current through the channel runs fast and brown.

choices.label: Swim the channel yourself
choices.intent: Wade in before he can, swim for the purse, and hand the tokens to his family.
choices.risk: This channel has drowned stronger swimmers than either of you.

success.text: You drag yourself onto the far pier half drowned, chest heaving, and cut the purse loose. The father weeps when you press the tokens into his hands, and the crews pay out their bets in sour silence.

failure.text: The current turns you twice and spits you onto a gravel bar far downstream, coughing up river water. When you limp back, the father is standing at the edge again, ready to try.

choices.label: Pay the family's fare
choices.intent: Trade the ferry crew enough of your food to carry the father and children across.
choices.risk: Your pack will be light for the road ahead.

success.text: The father keeps his boots on. He stares at you as though waiting for the price, and when none comes he herds his children aboard without looking back.

choices.label: Watch how the crews win
choices.intent: Study the channel and the crews until you see why nobody ever reaches the purse.
choices.risk: The crews do not like their game watched.

success.text: A rope under the surface runs from the pier to a crewman's hand, and he jerks the purse away whenever a swimmer gets close. You cut it in full view, and the father swims the channel clean.

failure.text: You stare at the water until a crewman notices and shoves you off the pier into the shallows. You climb out bruised and dripping, and by then the father has already gone in.

newCards.title: The Notice on the Post
newCards.flavor: A notice nailed to the landing post warns of fever on the far bank and closes the crossing until further word. Travelers read it, curse, and turn back toward the dry country. You saw the young ferry hand who nailed it up at dawn, and the far bank, as far as you can see, is busy and healthy.

choices.label: Ask the ferry hand why
choices.intent: Find the young ferry hand alone and ask him what the notice is really for.
choices.risk: A frightened liar may run, or may fight.

success.text: He whispers that the wardens across the river are taking new arrivals for gate labor, and the notice is the only warning he dared post. You leave it standing, and your road ahead bends north to a ford they do not watch.

failure.text: He bolts at your first question and knocks you into the post on his way past. By the time you pick yourself up, bruised, the notice has been torn down and he is gone.

choices.label: Tear down the notice
choices.intent: Rip the notice off the post and tell the turned-back travelers the far bank is clear.
choices.risk: Lies are usually posted for a reason.

success.text: The travelers believe you and crowd onto the next ferry, thanking you. From the far bank you watch wardens sort them into lines by the gatehouse, and you understand too late what the notice was for.

failure.text: Nobody believes a stranger over a nailed notice. They trudge back toward the dry country, and the ferry hand who posted it gives you a long, grateful look you do not understand until much later.

choices.label: Take the empty ferry
choices.intent: Pay your fare while the line is short and cross before anyone else reads the post.
choices.risk: Empty ferries leave from landings that know something.

success.text: The pilot takes your fare without meeting your eyes. On the far bank wardens are sorting new arrivals into work gangs, and you slip along the reeds and around them before anyone asks your name.

failure.text: On the far bank a warden takes your name and sets you hauling gate chain until dusk. He lets you go with aching shoulders and a long look that says he will know you again.

newCards.title: Chalk Prices on the Slate
newCards.flavor: Behind the counter, a slate lists the day's prices in fresh chalk. Each time the door opens, the trader glances at the newcomer's boots and pack, licks his thumb, and rewrites a number. When you walked in, the price of flour doubled, and the woman behind you, with a baby on her hip, has not yet reached the counter.

choices.label: Look like you can wait
choices.intent: Lean on the counter like someone with full saddlebags and nowhere to be.
choices.risk: Hunger shows in the eyes, however you stand.

success.text: You yawn at the flour price and ask after the weather. The trader wipes the slate and halves the number, and you leave with a full sack while, behind you, he chalks it higher for the woman with the baby.

failure.text: Your stomach growls in the silence, loud as a dropped pan. The trader smiles and chalks the price higher still, and you pay more than the flour is worth, because the road ahead is long.

choices.label: Work out how he prices
choices.intent: Watch the next three customers and learn exactly what makes the chalk move.
choices.risk: The trader notices people who watch instead of buy.

success.text: It is the boots: worn soles pay double, new leather pays half. You borrow a drover's good boots for an hour and buy flour for yourself and the woman with the baby at the lower price.

failure.text: You watch long enough for the trader to send his nephew to stand at your elbow. You buy nothing, and the long walk to the next well on an empty stomach leaves you light-headed and weak.

choices.label: Read the prices aloud
choices.intent: Read every price on the slate out loud, along with what each one said an hour ago.
choices.risk: A trader who sets the price can also refuse the sale.

success.text: The room goes quiet, then mutters. The trader wipes the slate clean and chalks one price for everyone, low enough to keep the crowd off his counter, and the woman with the baby leaves with a full sack.

failure.text: The trader refuses to sell to you at any price and has his nephew walk you out. Through the window you watch the woman with the baby pay double, as though your noise had been added to her bill.

choices.label: Pay for her flour
choices.intent: Set your own goods on the counter for the woman's flour before he can rewrite the price.
choices.risk: Your own sack will be lighter for it.

success.text: The trader shrugs and fills her sack. She looks at you as if you might want something from her later, and when you don't, she cries a little, quickly, and goes.

newCards.title: The Widow's Debt for Sale
newCards.flavor: The trader is auctioning a dead ferryman's debts off his counter, all of them written on one folded sheet. Whoever buys the sheet can collect from the widow, who stands by the door with her hands knotted in her apron. A land agent in a good coat has opened the bidding low, and he is already looking past her, at her land.

choices.label: Buy the debt and burn it
choices.intent: Outbid the land agent with most of your pack, then feed the sheet to the stove.
choices.risk: You will walk the next stretch hungry.

success.text: The sheet curls black in the stove while the room watches. The widow does not thank you; she asks, very quietly, what you want for it, and does not believe you when you say nothing.

choices.label: Bid up the land agent
choices.intent: Drive the bidding high with offers you cannot cover, then drop out and let him overpay.
choices.risk: If he drops out first, the debt is yours.

success.text: The agent pays three times what the sheet is worth, sweating, and the delighted trader slides you a sack of dried beans. The widow still owes the debt, but the agent has spent too much to buy her land as well.

failure.text: The agent smiles and lets you have it. You empty half your pack onto the counter to cover a bid you never meant to win, and walk out holding a debt you cannot bring yourself to collect.

choices.label: Ask to read the sheet
choices.intent: Ask aloud to read the debts before anyone bids, as any careful buyer would.
choices.risk: The trader wrote it, and he will not like this.

success.text: The figures are in the trader's hand, not the ferryman's, and half are for goods sold after the funeral. The room sees it too. The auction breaks up, and the widow walks out owing only what is honest.

failure.text: Every line looks honest to you, and you hand the sheet back. The land agent wins it for a song, and the widow slips out the door before the bidding is even done.

choices.label: Buy the debt to collect
choices.intent: Win the sheet cheaply and take your payment from the widow in food, as the paper allows.
choices.risk: Rights on paper sit badly with the people watching.

success.text: The agent shrugs and lets you have it. The widow pays you from her root cellar, sack by sack, never once looking at you, and you leave the post heavier than you came.

failure.text: The agent outbids you at the last call, and your bluster is spent for nothing. The widow saw what you meant to do, and so did everyone else in the room.

newCards.title: The Forged Water Ticket
newCards.flavor: The trading post sells water by the ticket, a stamped square of tin for each jug drawn from its cistern. A boy of about ten holds one up to the clerk, and it is plainly hammered out of a can lid. The clerk turns to you, standing closest, and asks whether the boy's ticket looks like yours.

choices.label: Swear the ticket is good
choices.intent: Hold your own ticket beside his and swear the two came from the same stamp.
choices.risk: If the clerk looks closely, you both lose your water.

success.text: The clerk squints, shrugs, and fills the boy's jug. He runs off sloshing it, and you never learn whose thirst he was carrying it home to.

failure.text: The clerk sets the two tickets side by side and keeps both. The boy is gone before anyone can grab him, and you walk on to the next well with an empty skin and a dry throat.

choices.label: Tell the clerk the truth
choices.intent: Say plainly that the ticket is a can lid, because it is, and the cistern is low.
choices.risk: The boy will know who said it.

success.text: The clerk thanks you with an extra measure in your skin and sends the boy away empty-handed. He does not cry. He looks at you once, the way people look at weather, and goes.

choices.label: Give him your own ticket
choices.intent: Press your real ticket into his hand and pocket the can lid yourself.
choices.risk: The next well is a long way off.

success.text: The boy's jug is filled, and he leaves at a run. The can lid stays in your pocket, and you walk to the next well with your own skin empty and the sun on your neck.

newCards.title: Fever Bark at Triple Price
newCards.flavor: A mother asks the trader the price of fever bark, and he names it. When she adds that it is for her son, who has burned for three days, the trader picks up his chalk and triples the number. The bark sits in a glass jar on the high shelf, and he keeps one hand on the counter near his cudgel.

choices.label: Haggle for her
choices.intent: Step in as her cousin and haggle the trader down as though the boy were family.
choices.risk: He may decide you are worth gouging too.

success.text: You find his soft spot: he hates a scene in front of paying customers. He sells her the bark at the first price, and she takes it and runs without a backward look.

failure.text: He sees through the cousin story at once and adds your name to the bill. You pay part of it from your own pack so she can leave with a single strip of bark.

choices.label: Pay the tripled price
choices.intent: Empty most of your pack onto the counter so the mother can take the bark now.
choices.risk: You will be the one going hungry this week.

success.text: The trader sweeps your goods into a bin and hands down the jar without a word. The mother clutches it and runs, and you walk out with your pack light and tomorrow already worrying you.

choices.label: Lift a strip from the jar
choices.intent: Wait for the trader to turn toward the stove, then take bark from the jar.
choices.risk: The cudgel is never far from his hand.

success.text: You slip one strip into the mother's basket as she leaves and pocket a second for the road. The trader counts his jar that night and never learns whom to blame.

failure.text: The jar lid scrapes, and the cudgel cracks across your forearm before you can pull back. He throws you out, and the mother leaves after you with nothing.

choices.label: Lean on the trader
choices.intent: Let him see in your face that you have hurt people before, and would again.
choices.risk: Frightened men make enemies who wait for a better day.

success.text: He looks at your hands, then your eyes, and sells her the bark at a fair price. As you leave, you hear him telling his nephew to describe your face to the wardens.

failure.text: He reaches the cudgel first, and the blow across your ribs tells you he has hurt people too. You stagger out, and the mother follows you, empty-handed.

newCards.title: The Deserter Behind the Bins
newCards.flavor: Behind the trading post, between three grain bins, a boy in a torn warden's coat crouches with his knees to his chest. The trader finds you looking and says there is a bounty on deserters, paid in flour. He will split it with you if you help hold the boy until the wardens ride through at dusk.

choices.label: Help hold the deserter
choices.intent: Pin the boy against the bins with the trader until the wardens arrive.
choices.risk: Cornered people fight harder than they look.

success.text: The boy fights like a cornered thing and then stops. At dusk the wardens take him in chains, and the trader weighs out your half of the flour with a satisfied nod.

failure.text: He bites, twists, and is over the fence, leaving you with a bleeding hand and the trader's contempt. The wardens arrive at dusk to find only you, and they take a good look.

choices.label: Hide him in the grain
choices.intent: Tell the trader the boy ran, then bury him to the neck in the middle bin.
choices.risk: Wardens probe grain bins with spears.

success.text: The wardens jab the first bin and the last, curse the trader, and ride off. At midnight the boy climbs out shaking flour from his hair and tells you a way through the delta no warden walks, and your road bends to it.

failure.text: A spear finds the middle bin. The boy is dragged out, and you are dragged with him, and you leave with a split lip and a warden who will know you anywhere.

choices.label: Give him food and leave
choices.intent: Push a day's food into his hands, say nothing to the trader, and walk away.
choices.risk: Food will not outrun the wardens for him.

success.text: You never learn whether he ran or was caught. The trader watches you go with narrowed eyes, and the offer of a split is not made to you again.

choices.label: Draw the wardens off
choices.intent: They already know your face, so let them chase you down the river road instead.
choices.risk: The wardens know the river road better than you do.

success.text: You let a warden glimpse you at dusk and run until your lungs burn. By the time they give up, the boy is far into the reeds, and your legs shake for an hour afterward.

failure.text: They ride you down at the river and beat you in the shallows before letting you go. Whether the boy got away, nobody at the post will tell you.

newCards.title: Two Maps, One Channel
newCards.flavor: Two families stand on either side of a new channel that cut through the delta overnight, each holding a map that puts the water on their claim. Neither map agrees with the riverbed, and both families are thirsty. They ask you, a stranger with no stake in it, to say whose water it is.

choices.label: Split the channel fairly
choices.intent: Pace off the channel and mark a line down the middle that both families can see.
choices.risk: A fair split can leave both sides short and angry.

success.text: You drive a stake at the middle and make each father put a hand on it. Neither family is happy and both have water, and the grandmother on the east side quietly hands you a cake of pressed dates.

failure.text: Both families take your line as an insult. The argument turns to shoving, and an elbow catches you in the jaw before they pull apart, each still claiming every drop.

choices.label: Side with the larger family
choices.intent: Give the water to the family with more children, because there it saves the most.
choices.risk: The smaller family has the sharper knives.

success.text: Your ruling stands. The smaller family packs their wagon that night and heads into the dry country, and the larger family's grandmother insists you share their supper before you go.

failure.text: The smaller family's eldest son draws on you before you finish speaking. You walk away with a cut forearm and leave the two families to settle it however they will.

choices.label: Read the old river signs
choices.intent: Use what you know of the old riverbeds to see where this channel will run next.
choices.risk: Read it wrong, and both families dig in the wrong place.

success.text: The channel is following a riverbed older than either map, and it will fork within the week, onto both claims. You show them the signs, and as you leave you see your own road ahead has shifted with the water.

failure.text: You read a bend that is not there. Both families dig where you point, strike only dry silt, and demand your water skin for their trouble, and you hand it over.

choices.label: Refuse to judge it
choices.intent: Tell them a stranger's word is worth nothing here, and walk on before you must choose.
choices.risk: Without a judge, they may settle it with knives.

success.text: Behind you the voices rise and then go quiet in a way you do not like. You do not turn around, and by the next rise the delta has hidden both families from view.

newCards.title: A Riverboat on Dry Sand
newCards.flavor: A paddle steamer sits upright on the cracked delta floor, a mile from any water, its wheel caked with dried mud. The captain still lives aboard and charges travelers a cup of grain for an hour in its shade. Her crew of four is thin as rope, and she will not let them go, because a captain does not abandon a boat that might still float.

choices.label: Tell the captain the truth
choices.intent: Sit with the captain in the shade and tell her the river is not coming back.
choices.risk: She has heard it before, and it made her angry.

success.text: She listens for a long time, then rings the ship's bell once and releases her crew. They walk off toward the ferry together, and she stays aboard alone, polishing the brass on the wheel.

failure.text: She orders you off her deck, and her crew throws you down the gangplank, apologizing as they do it. You land hard in the cracked mud and limp away.

choices.label: Trade for her river charts
choices.intent: Offer food for the captain's old charts, which show channels nobody has mapped in years.
choices.risk: Old charts may lead where the water left long ago.

success.text: Her charts show a dead channel that still runs underground and surfaces near the gate. The road you meant to take no longer makes sense, so you fold the charts away and turn toward a better one.

failure.text: The charts are beautiful and useless, drawn for a river that left before you were born. The captain keeps your food and wishes you luck with them, and she seems to mean it.

choices.label: Lead the crew off at night
choices.intent: Wait for dark, then guide the four crew past the captain's lantern to the ferry road.
choices.risk: The captain sleeps lightly and keeps an old pistol.

success.text: You lead four shadows across the moonlit flats and onto the ferry road by dawn. They split their last biscuits with you, and none of them looks back at the boat.

failure.text: The captain's lantern swings toward you, and the crew freezes, then climbs back aboard one by one. You stumble away alone in the dark, scraping your shins raw on the cracked ground.

choices.label: Pay for an hour's shade
choices.intent: Pay the captain her cup of grain and rest out the worst of the heat beneath the hull.
choices.risk: The crew is hungry, and you are carrying food.

success.text: In the hull's shade you sleep soundly for the first time in two days. You wake rested to find a crewman watching your pack the way hungry people watch, and you leave before you have to decide anything.

newCards.title: The Dowser's Forked Stick
newCards.flavor: A dowser walks the cracked delta with a forked willow stick held out before her, and a line of thirsty homesteaders follows at a respectful distance. When the stick dips, they dig, and they pay her a day's food for every dip. You notice that it only dips where the salt crust is thinnest, and that she always glances at the ground first.

choices.label: Show them what she reads
choices.intent: Tell the homesteaders she is reading the salt crust, and show them how to read it too.
choices.risk: Whatever the stick does, she is still finding them water.

success.text: The homesteaders crowd around as you point out the thin crust and the darker silt. By evening they are finding wet ground on their own, and the dowser sits alone on a rock, holding a stick nobody wants.

failure.text: The homesteaders want water today, not a stranger's theory. The dowser's eldest son walks you to the edge of camp by the collar, and his last shove puts you face-down and bruised in the salt.

choices.label: Ask her to teach you
choices.intent: Find the dowser alone at dusk and ask, plainly, to learn what she really reads.
choices.risk: Secrets that feed a family are not given away cheaply.

success.text: She laughs, then teaches you: thin crust, dark silt, reeds that lean toward water nobody can see. You walk on knowing where the river hides, and the route ahead rearranges itself in your mind.

failure.text: She charges you a day's food for the lesson and teaches you nothing the stick did not already show. Afterward you cannot tell whether she lied or you simply failed to understand.

choices.label: Pay her fee for a family
choices.intent: Pay the dowser's fee for the poorest family in the line, who cannot pay at all.
choices.risk: The stick may dip on nothing.

success.text: The stick dips for them beside a clump of dead reeds, and by sundown they have a muddy seep. The father offers to dig for you next, but you have nowhere here to stay.

newCards.title: A Dam of Broken Wagons
newCards.flavor: Upstream of the dry delta, squatters have built a dam of five broken wagon beds, stacked and packed with mud, to hold the last of the trickle for their camp. Their children splash in the little pond behind it. Downstream the reed beds are turning brown, and the delta farmer who walked up with you grips a crowbar.

choices.label: Break the dam open
choices.intent: Take the farmer's crowbar and pry the middle wagon bed out of the dam.
choices.risk: The squatters will not stand by and watch.

success.text: The wagon bed tears loose and the pond pours downstream in a brown rush that cuts across the road ahead, changing its course. The squatters' children stand in the mud where their pond was.

failure.text: Three squatters pull you off the dam before the bed moves, and they hit like people defending their children. You limp back downstream with the farmer, both of you bloodied.

choices.label: Broker a sharing schedule
choices.intent: Propose that the dam opens every other morning, and get both camps to swear to it.
choices.risk: Thirsty people make promises they cannot keep.

success.text: It takes all afternoon and two near-fights, but the squatters agree to pull one wagon bed every second morning. The farmer gives you a strip of dried squash for your trouble.

failure.text: Both sides agree, and you watch them break the agreement within the hour, each blaming the other. You leave hoarse and spent, with nothing settled behind you.

choices.label: Stay and dig a channel
choices.intent: This time you do not walk away; you dig a side channel so both camps share the trickle.
choices.risk: Digging in this heat can break anyone.

success.text: You dig for two days beside squatters and farmers alike until a side channel carries half the trickle around the dam. When you finally leave, sore to the bone, both camps walk you to the road.

failure.text: The ground is harder than your will, and on the second day you cannot lift the shovel. The channel is half dug when you leave, exhausted, and maybe someone will finish it.

choices.label: Fill your skins and go
choices.intent: Fill your skins from the squatters' pond while everyone argues, and go on your way.
choices.risk: The farmer walked up here trusting you.

success.text: Nobody stops you, because nobody is watching you at all. You walk downstream with full skins past the dying reeds, and the farmer's voice follows you a long way.

newCards.title: The Patrol's Strongbox
newCards.flavor: Half buried in a dry channel lie the remains of the missing river patrol: four rusted badges, a capsized skiff, and an iron strongbox still locked. The toll money inside was bound for the Crossing Gate. A scrap of oilcloth nailed to the skiff's ribs lists four names, with a request in faded ink that someone carry the badges home.

choices.label: Carry the badges home
choices.intent: Gather the four badges and the list and take the long detour back to the landing.
choices.risk: The detour is long, and grief is heavy to deliver.

success.text: The detour costs you a day's food, and at the landing you knock on four doors. Three families thank you; the fourth closes the door in your face, and you cannot blame her.

choices.label: Break open the strongbox
choices.intent: Pound the rusted lock with a stone until it gives, and take what the patrol died guarding.
choices.risk: Toll money is counted, and someone will come looking.

success.text: The lock gives on the twentieth blow. Inside are tokens enough to buy food at any post on the river, and you trade a handful at the next one for dried meat, knowing exactly whose money it is.

failure.text: The lock holds, and a shard of rust drives into your palm; by evening the wound is hot and swollen. You leave the box where it lies.

choices.label: Follow their last route
choices.intent: Read the skiff's position and the dried channel to learn what killed the patrol.
choices.risk: Whatever caught them may still be out here.

success.text: The channel turned under them overnight and left them stranded in salt. The same channel runs on, dry and hidden, toward the Crossing Gate, and your road ahead bends to follow it.

failure.text: You follow the dry channel too far, and the afternoon sun finds you with no shade and a skin you have to drain. You stagger back to the skiff at dusk, dizzy and scorched.

choices.label: Haul the box to the gate
choices.intent: Drag the strongbox to the Crossing Gate and hand the keeper what his patrol died for.
choices.risk: Iron is heavy, and the keeper may ask how you found it.

success.text: You arrive with raw hands and an aching back. The toll keeper opens the box with his own key, counts every token twice, and without a word of thanks writes your name on the page where debts are cleared.

newCards.title: Six Tally Sticks
newCards.flavor: Six split tally sticks hang from a nail outside the foreman's shed, one for each debtor still cutting stone. A young marmot named Pell holds the matching half of hers and asks you to lay it against his. Hers has nine notches. His has fourteen, and the foreman is watching from the doorway with his arms folded.

choices.label: Point out the false notches
choices.intent: Lay both halves side by side and show the foreman where his notches run past hers.
choices.risk: He decides what counts as true at this quarry.

success.text: The split lines up, and every laborer in earshot sees the five extra cuts. The foreman shaves them off with his knife, slowly, and you know he will remember your face longer than Pell's debt.

failure.text: He snaps Pell's half across his knee and says the shed's half is the only one that ever counted. His crew walks you to the quarry rim, none too gently, and you go down the slope bruised.

choices.label: Work a shift on her debt
choices.intent: Take up a hammer and cut stone in Pell's place until the foreman shaves one notch.
choices.risk: A day in the pit takes more than a day from you.

success.text: By dusk your hands are raw and your back is one long ache. The foreman shaves a single notch from Pell's stick, so she still owes thirteen, and she grips your hand and swears she will not forget it.

choices.label: Burn the foreman's halves
choices.intent: Wait for the shed lamp to go out, then feed all six of his halves to the stove.
choices.risk: If he wakes, the company will call it theft.

success.text: The six sticks crackle down to ash before the coals go grey. At dawn nobody can say what anyone owes, and the laborers drift toward the road in twos and threes, fast and quiet.

failure.text: A floorboard gives you away. The foreman's shout brings his crew, and you break free with a split lip, knowing the company's riders will carry your description to the next camp before you reach it.

newCards.title: Four Lamps on the Ledge
newCards.flavor: After dark, four lamps flicker along a ledge of the abandoned quarry, and a crew of debtors cuts stone by their light with no timbers under the shelf. Their boss, a badger named Orrin, says the company pays night crews double because the pit is condemned by day. If anyone reports them, they lose the only wage they have left.

choices.label: Show them how to set props
choices.intent: Spend the night cutting props from scrap timber and teaching the crew to wedge them.
choices.risk: Dead wood and tired hands make poor supports.

success.text: By the last lamp, three props stand under the worst of the shelf, and Orrin leans on each before he trusts it. He has no food to spare, only his word that the crew will stand by you if you ever need them.

failure.text: A prop splits as you hammer it home, and a slab drops past close enough to graze your arm. Orrin pulls you clear, and the crew goes back to cutting the way they always have.

choices.label: Put out the four lamps
choices.intent: Snuff the lamps and tell the crew the shelf will kill them before the debt does.
choices.risk: Hungry people do not thank you for their safety.

success.text: The last flame dies and the ledge goes black. In the dark Orrin admits he has buried two cutters already, and the crew climbs down with empty hands and lives they did not expect to keep.

failure.text: Someone relights a lamp as fast as you snuff one, and a cutter shoves you off the ledge onto the scree. You limp away with the sound of hammers still ringing behind you.

choices.label: Take a lamp and cut
choices.intent: Join the night crew for one shift and collect the double wage like everyone else.
choices.risk: The shelf above you has no props either.

success.text: You cut until your arms shake and stone dust coats your throat. At dawn the paymaster counts out company bread for your shift, and nobody on the crew asks why a stranger needed it.

choices.label: Lead them out the old adit
choices.intent: Guide the crew through the forgotten drainage adit you know of, out past the company's road.
choices.risk: Old tunnels flood without warning in storm season.

success.text: You find the adit mouth behind a fall of scree, and the crew follows you through it carrying all four lamps. It opens on a goat track the company never mapped, and the road ahead of you runs a different way now.

failure.text: Water has risen in the old adit, and you wade through it, cold enough to make you stagger. You bring the crew back to the ledge exhausted, and one by one they light their lamps again.

newCards.title: Three Bottles of Tonic
newCards.flavor: A peddler sets three bottles of tonic on a slab at the quarry rim, and the cutters line up, coughing grey dust into their sleeves. When he uncorks one you smell sugar, cheap spirits and enough poppy to make a sick body sleep. It cures nothing, and it is the only rest these workers get.

choices.label: Name what is in the bottles
choices.intent: Tell the line of cutters exactly what they are paying a day's wage to drink.
choices.risk: They may hate you more than the man who cheated them.

success.text: The line breaks up in angry muttering, and the peddler packs his slab before the first stone flies. That night you hear the cutters coughing in the dark, awake, and every one of them knows who told them.

failure.text: A gaunt cutter tells you to mind your own lungs, and the line closes against you. Someone shoves you hard into the slab, and the peddler sells all three bottles while you pick yourself up.

choices.label: Brew a real chest remedy
choices.intent: Steep the herbs you carry into a chest tea that loosens the dust instead of hiding it.
choices.risk: Your herbs may not stretch to every cough in line.

success.text: The cutters drink it bitter and hot, and by evening the worst of them coughs up grey clots and breathes easier. They have no coin for you, only the hoarse thanks of people who expected none.

failure.text: The tea comes out too weak, and the coughing barely changes. The peddler laughs and sells his bottles anyway, while you scrape the last of your herbs into a pot that does no good.

choices.label: Buy one for the worst cough
choices.intent: Trade food for one bottle and give it to the cutter who can no longer stand straight.
choices.risk: It buys one night of sleep and nothing more.

success.text: The old cutter drinks half and sleeps sitting up against the slab, breathing slow for the first time in days. In the morning he will cough again, and you are a meal lighter for one quiet night.

choices.label: Take a cut of his trade
choices.intent: Vouch for the tonic as a traveler who has seen it work, in return for a share.
choices.risk: Sick people remember who lied to them.

success.text: You tell the line what it wants to hear, and the last bottles sell faster than he can pour. Behind the slab the peddler slips you a parcel of dried meat, and the cutters thank you on their way back to the pit.

failure.text: A cutter's daughter sees the parcel change hands and shouts it down the line. The crowd drives you off the rim with stones, and you go down the slope bruised and empty-handed.

newCards.title: The Bell in the Sealed Adit
newCards.flavor: A bell hangs on a rope above a collapsed adit, and every hour, from somewhere under the rubble, someone pulls it. The company clerk says the tunnel was sealed a month ago with six cutters inside, and that digging will bring the hill down on the working face. He has already written all six names into the ledger of the dead.

choices.label: Dig toward the bell rope
choices.intent: Follow the rope down into the rubble and shift stone by hand toward whoever pulls it.
choices.risk: Every stone you lift loosens the one above it.

success.text: Your hands find a gap at last, and two thin arms reach through it. Four cutters crawl out into the daylight, and the eldest tells you they ate their candles to last. The clerk crosses out four names without a word.

failure.text: The pile shifts and pins you for a long, terrible minute before you wrench free. The bell goes on ringing beneath you, and you cannot make yourself climb back down.

choices.label: Find their air shaft
choices.intent: Walk the hillside above the adit, listening for where the bell's ringing leaks out of the ground.
choices.risk: The hillside is honeycombed, and not all of it holds.

success.text: Under a juniper you find an old air shaft breathing warm air, and you lower your own water down it on a cord. A voice answers, cracked and grateful, and now the clerk has no choice but to send diggers.

failure.text: The ground gives under you, and you slide into a rotten shaft, catching its lip with both hands. You haul yourself out scraped and shaking, and the ringing seems to come from everywhere at once.

choices.label: Let the ledger stand
choices.intent: Take the clerk at his word that digging would kill more than it saves, and walk on.
choices.risk: The bell will still be ringing as you leave.

success.text: You turn your back on the adit. The clerk thanks you for your good sense, and the working face keeps its crews and its wages. For the first mile you can still hear the bell, and then only the wind.

choices.label: Call in what you are owed
choices.intent: Send word to those who owe you, and ask them to bring shovels and timber.
choices.risk: Calling in a debt out here spends it for good.

success.text: By noon a dozen hands are passing stone down a line, setting props as they go. Five cutters come out alive and the hill holds. Whoever owed you owes you nothing now, and seems glad of it.

failure.text: Help comes late and in ones and twos, and the light is gone before anyone reaches the bell. You dig through the night beside them and leave at dawn exhausted, the ringing fainter than before.

newCards.title: The Company Store Scales
newCards.flavor: At the quarry rim the company store sells flour by the scoop, weighed on brass scales against two iron weights. A laborer's wife pays a week of scrip for a sack you can tell is light. The storekeeper, a tired hare with a bandaged hand, will not meet your eyes, and her own name is chalked on the debt board behind her.

choices.label: Call out the light sack
choices.intent: Weigh the woman's sack against your own known weight and say the number out loud.
choices.risk: The storekeeper takes the blame for the company's thumb.

success.text: The pan comes up short by a full quarter, and the line goes very quiet. The laborers get their flour weighed fair today. Tomorrow the company will send someone to ask the storekeeper why.

failure.text: The storekeeper insists the scales are true, her voice cracking, and the line sides with her over a stranger. You leave with the laborers' suspicion following you down the road.

choices.label: File the weights at night
choices.intent: Slip into the store after dark and file the iron weights down to honest heft.
choices.risk: A creaking board, and you are the thief.

success.text: You file by touch until both weights balance your own. Nobody will know why the sacks got heavier, and the storekeeper, finding iron filings on the counter at dawn, sweeps them up and says nothing.

failure.text: The storekeeper is asleep behind the counter, and she wakes with a club in her good hand. You take a blow across the back getting out the door, and her shouting follows you up the road.

choices.label: Make up the short weight
choices.intent: Pour flour from your own pack into the woman's sack until it weighs what she paid for.
choices.risk: Next week the sack will be light again.

success.text: She looks at the flour, then at you, and ties the sack shut before you can change your mind. Behind the counter the storekeeper turns away. Next week's sack will be just as light.

choices.label: Ask who set the weights
choices.intent: Wait until the line is gone, then ask the storekeeper quietly who set those weights.
choices.risk: She has more to lose by telling you than by lying.

success.text: She unwraps her hand to show you the brand the company gave her for weighing fair once. Then she draws you the back trail the ore wagons use, and the road ahead looks different than it did this morning.

failure.text: She tells you the weights came from the company, and the company is never wrong, and then she bars the door. Through the shutters you watch her sit and hold her bandaged hand for a long time.

newCards.title: The Cart in the Dry Wash
newCards.flavor: A family has camped in the bed of a dry wash beside their cart, its axle snapped and its bed piled with everything they own. Upstream, black clouds stand over the mesa, and the sand at your feet is already damp. The father, a lean pronghorn, will not leave the cart, because without it they have nothing to start over with.

choices.label: Lever the cart up the bank
choices.intent: Wedge a pole under the broken axle and drag the cart up onto the high bank.
choices.risk: The water may come before the cart moves.

success.text: The cart groans up the bank a hand's width at a time and tips onto high ground as the first brown water slides down the wash. The father sits on the tailboard and weeps, and the mother hands you a heel of bread.

failure.text: The pole snaps and the cart slams back into the sand. The flood knocks you flat while you are still hauling, and you crawl out bruised as the cart rolls away and the water cuts a new channel across the road ahead.

choices.label: Talk them out of the wash
choices.intent: Tell the father his children are the only cargo worth saving, and mean it.
choices.risk: He may hear a stranger telling him to give up.

success.text: He looks at the clouds, then at his children, and lifts the youngest down himself. From the high bank you all watch the water take the cart, the bedding, the seed sacks, everything. Nobody thanks you, and nobody needs to.

failure.text: He will not hear it, and you will not leave them. When the water comes you drag the smallest child up the bank yourself, soaked and gasping, while the father clings to the cart until the last moment.

choices.label: Read the flood sign
choices.intent: Watch the foam and drift upstream to judge how long you have before the water comes.
choices.risk: Desert floods move faster than any sign you trust.

success.text: The foam is slow and the clouds are farther off than they look, so you have an hour. You splint the axle with a tent pole, and the family rolls out on a side trail you would never have noticed, which changes the road ahead for you too.

failure.text: You misjudge the sign, and the water arrives in a roaring brown wall while you are still in the wash. You scramble out half-drowned and shaking, and the family's cart goes past you upside down.

newCards.title: Five Fallen Cairns
newCards.flavor: Five trail cairns lie kicked apart along the ledge, their stones scattered down the slope, and without them every fork looks the same. A ragged guide named Tamsin waits by the last one, offering to lead travelers through for a day's food. Her two children sit in the shade behind her, and there is fresh grit on the toes of her boots.

choices.label: Rebuild the five cairns
choices.intent: Gather the scattered stones and stack every cairn back where it stood for the next travelers.
choices.risk: The slope is loose, and Tamsin is watching you undo her living.
