success.text: By evening five cairns stand again, plain enough for anyone to follow. Tamsin gathers her children and walks off without a word, and you do not know where she will find tomorrow's food.

failure.text: A stone rolls out from under you and you slide down the scree, scraping your hands raw. When you climb back, Tamsin has already led the next family through, and the cairns lie where they fell.

choices.label: Pay Tamsin to guide you
choices.intent: Hand over a day's food and let her lead you, knowing exactly what she did.
choices.risk: You are paying for the harm, and the next family will too.

success.text: Tamsin leads you through without a wrong step, and she splits your food between her children before she eats. At the end of the ledge she says, not quite to you, that she would rather build cairns if anyone paid for those.

choices.label: Name what she has done
choices.intent: Tell Tamsin quietly that you know who kicked the cairns down, and ask her why.
choices.risk: Shamed people turn dangerous on a narrow ledge.

success.text: She does not deny it. Her husband died in the quarry owing the company, and the debt passed to her. She restacks the cairns herself while you watch, and asks you to say nothing at the camp ahead.

failure.text: She calls you a liar and sends her children up the slope with stones in their hands. You back away along the ledge, cut by a lucky throw, and pick your own slow way through the forks.

choices.label: Take the old scout line
choices.intent: Ignore the cairns and follow the older marks you learned to read, cut into the rock.
choices.risk: Old marks point to old trails, and old trails crumble.

success.text: The old notches lead up a chimney and across a mesa top no cairn has ever marked. Before you climb, you show Tamsin the marks, and the road ahead of you now runs where nobody below expects.

failure.text: The old marks end at a fall of fresh rock. You climb down the long way, exhausted, and find Tamsin waiting at the last cairn with the same offer as before.

newCards.title: The Raider Beneath the Arch
newCards.flavor: A storm is coming over the tablelands, and the only shelter for a mile is a stone arch with room beneath it for two. A wounded raider already lies there, a coyote with a broken leg and a caravan's stolen saddlebags under his head. He watches the lightning walk closer and says he will share if you will.

choices.label: Share the arch and your food
choices.intent: Crawl in beside him, splint his leg, and split your food with him through the storm.
choices.risk: He robbed people for a living, and he still can.

success.text: The storm roars for hours while you sit shoulder to shoulder with a thief, sharing your bread. At dawn he names the caravan he robbed and leaves the saddlebags for you to return, then limps off the other way.

choices.label: Take the saddlebags
choices.intent: Drag the stolen saddlebags out from under him and claim the arch for yourself.
choices.risk: Cornered thieves fight hardest.

success.text: He fights, but not for long. You sit out the storm under the arch with the saddlebags under your own head while he lies out in the rain. In the morning there is dried meat in the bags and nothing at all in his eyes.

failure.text: He has a knife you did not see, and it opens your arm before you wrestle it away. You both spend the storm under the arch, bleeding and not speaking.

choices.label: Ask about the missing caravans
choices.intent: Shelter beside him and work out, between thunderclaps, who he really rides for.
choices.risk: A clever thief will sell you a story for a dry place.

success.text: He rides for no one, and the travelers he meant to rob were turned back at the warden's bridge and kept there, not dead. Before he sleeps he scratches you the raiders' way around the bridge, and the road ahead shifts with it.

failure.text: He tells you a long, good story about a gang in the hills, and you believe it until he slips away in the last of the rain with your waterskin. You wake cold, thirsty and alone.

newCards.title: The Writ and the Runaways
newCards.flavor: Two runaway quarry debtors crouch in a crack in the canyon wall, a mother and her grown son, begging you with their eyes not to look their way. Around the bend comes a bounty hunter holding a company writ with their names on it, signed and sealed. The debt is real, and so is the reward he offers for a pointed finger.

choices.label: Send him up the wrong fork
choices.intent: Look the hunter in the eye and swear you saw two figures heading for the north fork.
choices.risk: If he checks the dust, he will know who lied.

success.text: He touches his hat and takes the north fork at a trot. When he is gone the mother squeezes your hands, and her son shows you the side canyon they meant to take, so your road ahead changes with theirs. The writ will find them somewhere, but not today.

failure.text: He kneels, reads the tracks, and smiles at you without warmth. He walks them out of the crack in irons, and as he passes he promises the company will hear your name too.

choices.label: Point to the crack
choices.intent: Take the hunter's reward and show him where they hide, because the debt is real.
choices.risk: You will see their faces as he walks them past.

success.text: He pays in hard bread and dried fruit and walks the mother and son past you in irons. The son looks at you. The mother does not, and that is worse.

choices.label: Read the writ closely
choices.intent: Ask to see the writ, and look for a flaw in the company's seal or wording.
choices.risk: Bounty hunters do not like travelers who read.

success.text: The writ names a debt signed by the son, but by its own date he was a boy of twelve when the company took his mark. You say so loudly, finger on the date, and the hunter rolls the writ up slowly. He is not paid enough for this.

failure.text: The writ is clean, every seal in order. The hunter takes it back, takes his time finding them, and takes the cost of your delay out of you with the back of his hand.

choices.label: Trade on your bad name
choices.intent: Let the hunter recognize the face the wardens are hunting, and dare him to try you.
choices.risk: A hunter who knows your face may want both rewards.

success.text: He knows you, all right, and his eyes go to your hands and stay there. One writ is not worth a fight with someone the wardens could not hold, and he rides back the way he came. The runaways do not wait to thank you.

failure.text: He knows you, and he is not afraid. The fight is short and ugly, and when it ends he has the runaways and you have a split lip, an aching back and a second price on your name.

newCards.title: The Shrine at Whistling Notch
newCards.flavor: The wind screams through a notch in the mesa where the trail squeezes down to a single stride. At its mouth a shrine of piled stones holds tin cups of water and crusts of bread, and an old ewe sits beside it, counting under her breath. She says no one passes without an offering for the ones the notch has taken.

choices.label: Leave bread at the shrine
choices.intent: Set a crust of your own food among the others and wait for her nod.
choices.risk: It feeds no one but the ravens and the dead.

success.text: She nods and tells you to walk when she says seven. You go on her count, and the wind drops for exactly as long as it takes to cross. You do not know whether it was the bread or the counting.

choices.label: Count the gusts yourself
choices.intent: Sit beside her, learn the rhythm she is counting, and cross on the lull.
choices.risk: Wind on the mesa keeps no promises.

success.text: Seven gusts, then a hush long enough to cross. You walk the notch on the lull with your food untouched, and the old ewe watches you go as if you had stolen something from her.

failure.text: You start on what you take for the lull, and the eighth gust slams you into the wall. You crawl the rest of the notch on hands and knees, bruised and half deafened.

choices.label: Ask whom the notch took
choices.intent: Ask the old ewe whose names the shrine is for, and listen to the whole answer.
choices.risk: Grief does not always want company.

success.text: Her husband, her daughter, and eleven others she lists by name. When she finishes she shows you a goat path that climbs around the notch entirely, one she never shows anyone, and the road ahead bends away from the wind.

failure.text: She goes silent and does not speak again. You wait long enough to know you have intruded, then cross the notch without her count, and the wind batters you raw.

choices.label: Push through without paying
choices.intent: Brace against the rock and force your way through the notch on strength alone.
choices.risk: The wind has taken stronger walkers than you.

success.text: You lean into the wind and make it through, one handhold at a time. When you look back, the old ewe is setting out a fresh cup of water, and she does not look up.

failure.text: Halfway through, a gust lifts you off your feet and drops you hard on the rock. You make the far side aching with every breath, and her counting follows you on the wind.

newCards.title: One Pot, Seven Bowls
newCards.flavor: The camp cook ladles bean stew from one black pot into seven bowls lined up on a flat rock, and there is not enough to fill seven. Two more travelers have just come in out of the storm, a quarry widow and her small son. The cook looks at you, because you are the newest face at the fire, and someone has to go without.

choices.label: Give your bowl to the boy
choices.intent: Hand your bowl to the widow's son and go to your bedroll hungry.
choices.risk: Tomorrow's trail is long, and you will walk it empty.

success.text: The boy eats with both hands and falls asleep against his mother before the bowl is clean. You lie awake listening to your own stomach, weak and cold, and in the morning nobody mentions it.

choices.label: Stretch the stew
choices.intent: Add your own dried roots and canyon greens to the pot and cook it thin for nine.
choices.risk: Thin stew may leave everyone hungry instead of most.

success.text: The stew comes out thin but hot, and nine bowls go around instead of seven. The cook claps you on the back and gives you the scrapings from the bottom of the pot, which everyone knows are the best part.

failure.text: The greens you added are bitter enough to spoil the pot, and nobody eats well. The widow gives her share to her son anyway, and the camp eyes you sourly all night.

choices.label: Find who is hoarding
choices.intent: Watch the faces at the fire for whoever is sitting on food they will not share.
choices.risk: Accusing a fellow traveler can split a camp in a storm.

success.text: A trader by the far wall keeps his pack between his knees and will not meet anyone's eye. When you ask him quietly, he opens it on hard biscuit enough for everyone, and he passes it round with poor grace, one to you as well.

failure.text: You pick the wrong face. The old herder you question has nothing in his pack but his dead wife's shawl, and the camp does not forget it. You eat your thin share alone at the edge of the firelight.

choices.label: Tell them there is no room
choices.intent: Tell the widow the pot was made for seven, and the people already here come first.
choices.risk: The storm is still blowing beyond the firelight.

success.text: The cook does not argue. The widow takes her son back out into the wind without a word, and you eat your full bowl with the others, warm and rested, while the storm goes on.

newCards.title: Dice for an Indenture
newCards.flavor: A labor recruiter rolls three bone dice by the fire, and the stake in front of him is a signed indenture. A drifter barely grown has bet himself into five years at the quarry and lost it twice already. The recruiter offers to let you play for the paper, if you have something worth putting up.

choices.label: Play for the paper
choices.intent: Put up a share of your food and throw the bones against him for the drifter's paper.
choices.risk: The house rarely loses at its own fire.

success.text: Your third roll beats his, and the recruiter pushes the indenture across with a sour face. The drifter burns it himself, slowly, holding the paper until the flame reaches his fingers.

failure.text: His dice run hot all night, and more of your food goes into his sack along with the drifter's last hope. The recruiter thanks you for the game, and means it.

choices.label: Catch the loaded die
choices.intent: Watch how the recruiter palms and rolls until you see which die he favors.
choices.risk: Calling a cheat a cheat is how knives come out.

success.text: The third die always lands heavy. You pick it up before he can, split it on a rock, and show the camp the lead inside. The recruiter leaves the indenture in the dirt and is gone by morning.

failure.text: You call it and you are wrong, because the dice roll fair when the camp tests them. The recruiter's friends drag you from the fire and leave you to sleep cold and bruised.

choices.label: Buy out his five years
choices.intent: Offer the recruiter everything in your food sack for the paper, no dice involved.
choices.risk: It is most of what you have, spent on a stranger.

success.text: The recruiter weighs your sack, shrugs, and hands over the indenture. The drifter stares at you as if you might be a trick, and by morning he is gone, free of the paper and without a word of thanks.

newCards.title: A Letter for the Warden
newCards.flavor: An old woman by the fire presses a sealed letter into your hands and asks you to carry it to the Canyon Warden's bridge. Her son serves there as an escort and has not written in a year. She cannot read, so the camp scribe wrote it for her, and she wants your promise that you will not open it.

choices.label: Swear to carry it sealed
choices.intent: Tuck the letter inside your coat and give her your word it stays shut.
choices.risk: Whatever it says, you will be the one who delivered it.

success.text: She makes you say it twice, then pats the coat where the letter sits. All night she watches you from across the fire, as if afraid the paper might burn through. It weighs almost nothing.

choices.label: Lift the seal at night
choices.intent: Wait until she sleeps, then work the wax loose with a warm blade and read.
choices.risk: If she wakes, you will have broken more than wax.

success.text: The scribe has written more than her words. The missing travelers at the bridge are fevered and kept apart, the letter says, and the warden turns back anyone who might carry the sickness out. You reseal it carefully.

failure.text: The wax cracks in two, loud as a branch in the quiet. She is awake and looking at you, and she takes the letter back without a word and gives it to someone else in the morning.

choices.label: Ask who wrote it for her
choices.intent: Ask her gently who wrote the letter, and whether she knows what it says.
choices.risk: She may take the question for a refusal.

success.text: She knows every word. It says she forgives her son for leaving, that she is dying, and that he need not come. She wants him to come anyway, and she asks you to tell him so out loud.

failure.text: She takes the question as a refusal and gives the letter to a mule driver instead. You spend the evening watching it ride away in his saddlebag, carried by someone who will never ask.

choices.label: Add a line of your own
choices.intent: Ask the scribe to add a line from someone who once walked away and regretted it.
choices.risk: Your regret may not be welcome in her letter.

success.text: You tell the scribe what you left behind on the road, and he writes it down plainly beneath her words. The old woman listens, nods, and says her son will understand it better from a stranger.

failure.text: You start to tell it and find you cannot. The words stick, the scribe waits, and at last you shake your head. The old woman pats your hand as if you were the one in need.

newCards.title: The Thief at the Picket Post
newCards.flavor: The camp has tied a young otter to the picket post at the edge of the firelight, wrists bound and a stolen sack of meal at his feet. The storm is turning cold, and the camp means to leave him there until morning. He says nothing in his own defense, but he keeps looking past the fires toward the dark canyon mouth.

choices.label: Speak for him at the fire
choices.intent: Argue at the fire that a freezing night is too much punishment for a sack of meal.
choices.risk: Defending a thief makes you look like his partner.

success.text: The camp grumbles, but the cook cuts his ropes and sets him nearer the fire. He mumbles thanks into his knees. Before dawn he is gone, and so is the sack of meal, and nobody bothers to mention it to you.

failure.text: They hear you out and vote you down, and to make the point they give your blanket to his guard. You spend the night shivering beside the post with the boy, two fools in the cold.

choices.label: Look where he keeps looking
choices.intent: Slip out past the fires toward the canyon mouth to see what he keeps watching for.
choices.risk: The storm hides more than one hungry stranger.

success.text: In a hollow beyond the firelight you find his sister and his grandfather sharing a single wet blanket. You bring them in, and the camp, seeing them, unties the boy without a vote.

failure.text: The dark swallows the canyon mouth, and you stumble into a gully full of icy runoff. You come back soaked and exhausted, having found nothing, and the boy turns his face away.

choices.label: Pay for what he stole
choices.intent: Give the camp food from your own pack to cover the sack, and ask them to free him.
choices.risk: Paying a thief's debt teaches the camp that thieving pays.

success.text: The camp takes your food and cuts the ropes. The boy picks up the stolen sack, hesitates, and runs into the dark with it toward whatever he was watching for. You never learn what it was.

choices.label: Leave it to the camp
choices.intent: It is their camp and their meal, so go to your bedroll and let their rule stand.
choices.risk: You will hear him shivering all night.

success.text: You sleep badly. Twice you wake to the sound of the boy's teeth, and twice you turn over. At dawn they cut him loose, grey with cold, and he walks toward the canyon mouth without looking back.

newCards.title: Two Piles of Voting Stones
newCards.flavor: Thunder rolls down the canyon, and the camp has to choose: climb to the mesa top and risk the lightning, or stay below and risk the flood. Two piles of voting stones sit on a blanket, exactly even, white for climbing and black for staying. The camp boss hands you the last stone, because you are a stranger with nothing to gain.

choices.label: Read the storm first
choices.intent: Climb a little way up the wall to watch where the lightning strikes and the water runs.
choices.risk: Lightning finds whoever stands highest.

success.text: From the ledge you see the lightning working the far mesa and a brown line already creeping up the canyon floor. You drop a white stone, the camp climbs, and by morning the water has rearranged the road below and the landmarks ahead.

failure.text: A strike lands close enough to throw you off the ledge onto the scree. You stagger back to the blanket singed and deafened, and the camp votes without you.

choices.label: Watch the camp boss
choices.intent: While the camp argues, study the boss and work out why he handed you the stone.
choices.risk: Calling out the one who runs the fire can cost your place.

success.text: He keeps glancing at a cache of trade goods buried on the low side of camp. You say so aloud, the camp votes to climb without your stone, and the boss is left digging his goods out in the rain. He does not speak to you again.

failure.text: If he has a reason, you cannot find it, and the camp tires of your staring. Someone takes the stone from your hand and drops it on the black pile, and you spend a long, wet, sleepless night below.

choices.label: Refuse to cast the stone
choices.intent: Hand the stone back and tell them a stranger should not choose who drowns.
choices.risk: A camp that cannot decide will decide badly.

success.text: The boss pockets the stone and the vote stays even, so the camp splits. Half climb toward the lightning and half stay in the canyon, and you lie awake not knowing which half to hope for.

choices.label: Argue they move together
choices.intent: Tell the camp the worst choice is splitting up, and talk them onto one road.
choices.risk: Holding a frightened camp together takes more than words.

success.text: They throw the white stones and the black stones together into the fire, then climb as one, carrying the old ones between them. It is a hard, wet night, but at dawn everyone is still there to count.

failure.text: Your voice is lost under the thunder, and the camp breaks into shouting knots. You spend the night running messages between two halves who will not listen, and you meet the dawn exhausted.

newCards.title: The Fortieth Stone
newCards.flavor: A crow-witch sits cross-legged at the cave mouth with a clay bowl in her lap and one river stone in her hand. Thirty-nine stones already lie in the bowl, one for each breath the air below can carry, she says. Behind you, a young mother shields her baby from the sleet, and the witch's eyes move from her to you.

choices.label: Give the mother your place
choices.intent: Step back into the sleet and nod the mother toward the witch's last stone.
choices.risk: The storm outside has no shelter left in it.

success.text: The fortieth stone drops into the bowl and the mother slips past you into the dark. You spend the night wedged under a dripping ledge, shaking. At dawn a drover climbs out, and the witch lets you in with a single black feather and no word.

choices.label: Ask how she counts forty
choices.intent: Ask how she reckons forty breaths, and watch her face while she answers.
choices.risk: She may take doubt as an insult to the dead.

success.text: She tells you about the winter the air went bad and eleven sleepers never woke. The number is honest, but she was counting herself. She sets her own stone aside, walks out into the sleet, and lets you and the mother both pass.

failure.text: She hears the doubt and closes her hand around the last stone. The mother goes in; you do not. You shelter in a crack in the ridge until the hail passes and come in at dawn, stiff, soaked and hungry.

choices.label: Push past the witch
choices.intent: Shoulder past the witch and her bowl before the mother can reach the stone.
choices.risk: The witch has friends inside, and the dark is theirs.

success.text: She goes down hard against the rock and the bowl spills. You are inside before she can rise. Nobody stops you, but the mother's crying follows you a long way down the passage, and a sheltering family moves their blankets away from yours.

failure.text: Her stick cracks across your shins, and two crow-folk from inside haul you back out into the sleet, your shins bruised. When they let you in at dawn, every face at the fire already knows what you tried.

choices.label: Open the old wind-shaft
choices.intent: Lead the mother up to the old wind-shaft, which breathes into a chamber of its own.
choices.risk: The shaft is steep, and a baby cannot be dropped.

success.text: The shaft breathes cold, clean air, just as the old ways promised. You hand the baby down rung by rung, and the witch, hearing of it, sets a second bowl beside the first. The tunnels ahead open in a different order than the ones you planned on.

failure.text: The rungs are rotten halfway down. You catch the mother's arm and the baby both, and your shoulder takes all of it. You climb back out together, aching, and wait in the sleet for the witch's next empty place.

newCards.title: No Fever Past the Rope
newCards.flavor: A sentry has strung a rope across the cave mouth and hung a tin cup from it: anyone with fever waits outside. A carter with burning cheeks sits against the rock while his daughter holds the cup of rainwater to his mouth. Forty people share the air below, the sentry says, and last spring a fever took nine of them in a week.

choices.label: Vouch for the carter
choices.intent: Tell the sentry you will keep the carter apart from the others and answer for him.
choices.risk: If the fever spreads, the camp will blame you.

success.text: The sentry lifts the rope for you both, and you settle the carter in a dry side passage away from the others. The fever breaks by morning. His daughter brings you half a corn cake she must have been saving for herself.

failure.text: The sentry will not hear it, and the camp behind him mutters agreement. You sit out the night with the carter and his daughter under the dripping rock, and by dawn the cold has settled deep into your chest.

choices.label: Look closely at the fever
choices.intent: Study the carter's eyes, hands and breathing to learn what kind of sickness this is.
choices.risk: Some fevers pass from hand to hand.

success.text: It is not plague but a splinter gone bad under his thumbnail, red lines running up the wrist. You show the sentry, cut it clean, and he lets them in. Nobody thanks you, but nobody sends you away either.

failure.text: You cannot tell what it is, and you stay close too long trying. By evening your own head aches and your joints are heavy, though the fever never quite takes hold of you.

choices.label: Brew a fever draught
choices.intent: Steep the herbs you carry and dose him through the night at the rope's edge.
choices.risk: The herbs may not be strong enough for this.

success.text: By the small hours the carter is sweating and clear-eyed. The sentry has watched you work all night, and at dawn he lifts the rope himself. He tells you which passage the camp keeps for the sick, and which it keeps for the dead.

failure.text: The draught is not enough, and you burn through the last of your herbs trying. The carter lives, but only just, and you come away from the long night hollow-eyed and spent.

choices.label: Leave them food and go in
choices.intent: Accept the sentry's rule, press some food into the girl's hands, and go below.
choices.risk: Whatever happens to them out here, you won't see it.

success.text: The sentry nods you past. At the first bend you look back once: the girl is still holding the tin cup, and the food is already in her father's hands. Below, the air is close and warm, and you are glad of the rope.

newCards.title: A Loom Too Wide
newCards.flavor: A family's handcart is jammed in the cave mouth, its load a weaver's loom lashed upright and wider than the gap by a hand. Hail is walking down the ridge behind them. The grandmother will not cut it loose, because the loom is the only thing they own that earns, and the two boys pushing the cart are already blue with cold.

choices.label: Take the loom apart
choices.intent: Knock out the pegs and carry the loom through in pieces the grandmother can rebuild.
choices.risk: Lose one peg in the dark and it never weaves again.

success.text: The frame comes apart in your hands as if it wants to. The boys carry the beams, the grandmother counts every peg into her apron, and once inside she ties a strip of her best cloth around your wrist.

failure.text: A peg snaps and another rolls into a crack you cannot reach. The loom goes in crippled, and the hail catches you on the last trip, stinging your hands and neck raw.

choices.label: Ask what the loom means
choices.intent: Ask the grandmother what she is really afraid of losing, and listen for the true answer.
choices.risk: She may hear a stranger telling her to give up.

success.text: It was her mother's, she says, and the pattern on the beam was her mother's too. She cuts one finished length of cloth free, leaves the frame to the hail, and hurries the boys inside. She does not speak to you again.

failure.text: She hears only a stranger telling her to be poor. She sets her feet, the boys stay with her, and you spend an hour at their side, cold to the bone, until the hail passes and the cart can be tipped through.

choices.label: Shelter the boys yourself
choices.intent: Wrap the two boys in your coat and carry them in, leaving the argument outside.
choices.risk: The hail will have nothing between it and you.

success.text: You carry them in under your coat, one on each side, while the hail drums on your back. The grandmother follows them at last, without the loom. She will never forgive the cave, and a little of that falls on you.

choices.label: Shoulder the cart through
choices.intent: Put your back into the cart and drive it through the gap, loom and all.
choices.risk: Stone, loom or your back: something will break.

success.text: Wood shrieks against stone, and then the cart is through with one crossbar scraped white. The boys whoop. The grandmother cuts you a knot of dried mutton from her stores for the strength in your back.

failure.text: Something in your back gives before the stone does. The cart stays wedged until the hail passes, and you limp inside behind the family, sore from neck to knee.

newCards.title: The Creditor's Ledger
newCards.flavor: A storekeeper waits at the cave mouth with a ledger open on his knee and rain running off his hat brim. The Hallorans owe him a winter of flour, and he knows they fled into the dark. His own store burned in the same drought that ruined them, and he has three pages of debts like theirs and a wife coughing in his wagon.

choices.label: Send him the wrong way
choices.intent: Tell him the Hallorans took the ridge road west two days ago.
choices.risk: If he catches the lie, he'll go in angry.

success.text: He believes you, which is worse than you expected. He closes the ledger, thanks you, and turns his wagon toward the ridge, his wife coughing under the canvas. The family below will never know how close he came.

failure.text: He has heard that lie before, from better liars. He goes in with a lamp and a cudgel, and you spend the night standing between him and the Hallorans, taking one blow that was meant for the father.

choices.label: Broker new terms
choices.intent: Bring him and the Hallorans together and bargain for a debt they can actually pay.
choices.risk: Two frightened families in one room can turn ugly.

success.text: It takes half the night. The Hallorans will send him wool from their first flock, and he will not go to the county sheriff. He writes the terms in his ledger and asks you to sign as witness.

failure.text: Halloran's son spits at the storekeeper, the storekeeper strikes the boy, and you get a fist in the ribs pulling them apart. He leaves with nothing settled and their names underlined twice.

choices.label: Pay down the debt yourself
choices.intent: Give him what food you can spare against the Hallorans' page, so his wife eats tonight.
choices.risk: It won't clear the debt, and your pack will feel it.

success.text: He weighs your sack, crosses out a third of the Hallorans' page, and writes your mark beside it. It is not enough to clear them, and he says so. But his wife eats tonight, and so, below, do they.

choices.label: Stare him down
choices.intent: Let him see what kind of hands you have, and suggest he forget this page.
choices.risk: Frightened people sometimes come back with friends.

success.text: Something in your face tells him what you have already done on this road. He tears the page out himself and drives off fast, and you know he will tell the story in every town ahead. The Hallorans thank you from a careful distance.

failure.text: He is not as frightened as you need him to be. He swings the ledger's iron clasp into your jaw and drives off into the rain, shouting your description to every wagon he passes.

newCards.title: The Mule That Fears the Dark
newCards.flavor: Hail the size of knuckles is falling, and an old packer is hauling at a mule that will not step past the first shadow of the cave. Two sacks of flour ride on its back, meant for the families sheltering below. The packer is crying and swearing in the same breath, and the mule's flank is already striped with welts from the ice.

choices.label: Blindfold the mule
choices.intent: Tie your scarf over the mule's eyes so it cannot see the dark it fears.
choices.risk: A blind, frightened mule kicks at anything close.

success.text: The mule stands trembling, then lets you lead it in by the halter, one slow step at a time. Below, the packer scoops a cup of flour from the sack for you and will not take it back.

failure.text: The scarf slips at the first crack of hail and the mule kicks out blind, catching your leg. You get it inside eventually, limping, and the packer apologizes all the way down.

choices.label: Talk the mule in
choices.intent: Stand at the mule's head and talk low and steady until it trusts your voice.
choices.risk: The hail won't wait for it to trust you.

success.text: It takes a long time. Then the mule leans its head into your chest and walks in beside you, and the packer, wiping his face, presses a fist of dried apples on you. It has never done that for anyone but his dead wife, he says.

failure.text: The mule will not be talked to. The packer drags the sacks off and carries them in on his own back, three trips, while you hold the shaking animal under the overhang and the hail finds you.

choices.label: Cut the flour loose
choices.intent: Slash the straps, carry the flour in yourselves, and leave the mule to the storm.
choices.risk: The packer has had that mule half his life.

success.text: You cut the straps and haul the sacks in, two trips each. The mule bolts down the ridge into the hail and does not come back. The families below eat, and the packer sits apart from the fire and will not look at you.

newCards.title: The Guttering Debt Candle
newCards.flavor: In a niche of the candle court burns a stub of tallow with a dead man's name scratched into its base. Every unpaid oath keeps a candle here, the clerk explains, and when this one gutters, the debt passes to the man's daughter. She is twelve, and she sits before the flame cupping her hands around it, as if that could stop it burning down.

choices.label: Argue the law to the clerk
choices.intent: Tell the clerk an oath sworn by one person cannot bind a child who never spoke it.
choices.risk: The court does not like strangers explaining its rules.

success.text: The clerk hears you out, then sends for the adjudicator, who hears you out again. They agree, slowly, that the girl swore nothing. The candle is allowed to go out on its own, and the debt goes with it.

failure.text: The clerk reads you the court's oldest rule aloud, twice, and has you put out of the hollow to cool off. You wait in the cold passage until the chill is in your bones, and hear the girl begin to cry.

choices.label: Find the oath's exact words
choices.intent: Search the court's wax tablets for the exact words the dead man swore.
choices.risk: The clerks guard those tablets, and the wax is soft.

success.text: The oath was sworn until the thaw, and the thaw came two months ago. Time paid the debt in full. The clerk is embarrassed, the girl is free, and nobody offers you anything but a dry seat by the fire.

failure.text: A clerk catches you with your hand on the soft wax and shoves you hard against the niche. The tablets go back on the shelf, and your elbow will be stiff for days.

choices.label: Swear the debt onto yourself
choices.intent: Kneel at the niche and speak the dead man's oath in your own name instead of hers.
choices.risk: Oaths sworn in the hollow follow you farther than roads do.

success.text: The clerk scratches your mark beneath the dead man's name and takes two days of your food as the first payment. The girl stares at you as if you had walked out of the rock. The candle burns on, and now it is yours.

choices.label: Keep the vigil with her
choices.intent: Sit beside the girl through the night and shield the flame with your own hands.
choices.risk: Tallow spits, and the night is long.

success.text: You have walked away from someone before, and this time you stay. Your palms blister in the heat of the flame. When it gutters at dawn, the clerk writes the debt against her name, but she does not hear it alone.

newCards.title: The Drip-Pool Ration
newCards.flavor: One drip-pool feeds everyone sheltering in the hollow, and each family drinks by turn, a tin cup apiece, sworn on the stone. A newcomer drank out of turn in the night, two cups, for his sick wife. The oath-keepers have him by the arms at the passage mouth, ready to put him out into the storm, while the line at the pool watches in silence.

choices.label: Speak for him before the line
choices.intent: Remind the oath-keepers that anyone in that line would have done the same.
choices.risk: The thirsty are not always moved by fairness.

success.text: Someone in the line laughs, ashamed, and then another, and the keepers let him go with a lost turn as his penalty. His wife lives out the week. The keepers watch you now the way they watch him.

failure.text: The line closes against you both. The man is put out, and you go with him rather than watch, sitting out the storm at the passage mouth, chilled and aching, until the keepers relent at dawn.

choices.label: Give him your turns
choices.intent: Swear your own cups to his family for the next three days, so the debt is paid.
choices.risk: Three days is a long time without water.

success.text: The keepers accept it. For three days you drink only what drips off the walls into your palm, and your head swims by the second evening. The man brings you his wife's thanks and nothing else; he has nothing else.

choices.label: Search for another seep
choices.intent: Follow the damp along the hollow's walls to find water nobody has sworn over yet.
choices.risk: The deep rock does not give water up easily.

success.text: Behind a fall of slate you find a second trickle, thin but clean. Nobody needs to be put out tonight. The keepers swear it into the ration before you finish speaking and pour you the first full cup.

failure.text: You follow the damp into a crawl that narrows to nothing and scrape your hands raw backing out. When you return, the man is gone into the storm, and his wife is staring at the passage mouth.

choices.label: Stand surety for him
choices.intent: Swear on the stone that he will keep the ration, and stake your own word on it.
choices.risk: If he breaks it, the hollow will remember it was you.

success.text: Word has run ahead of you that your promises hold. The keepers let him go on your oath, and he keeps the ration after that, and so do you. Later his wife sends you the best of a meal they find.

failure.text: They take your oath, and he breaks it the next night, desperate. The keepers put him out and dock your own turn for the breach, and you go thirsty through a long day.

newCards.title: The Name Jar
newCards.flavor: A crow-witch sits on a salt barrel beside a clay jar sealed with wax, and a line of refugees waits before her. For one name spoken into the jar, she gives a wool blanket; the name goes in, and the speaker never remembers it again. The old man ahead of you is trying to choose between his brother and his first daughter.

choices.label: Speak a name into the jar
choices.intent: Give up one name you love so the old man can keep both of his.
choices.risk: Some losses you won't know the size of.

success.text: You lean close and say it. Afterward there is a smooth place in your memory where someone used to be, and you cannot find its edges. The old man takes the blanket from you with shaking hands and keeps his brother and his daughter.

choices.label: Bargain her down
choices.intent: Offer her a true story instead of a name, and argue it is worth more to a collector.
choices.risk: She knows the worth of names better than you do.

success.text: She listens to your story of the drought road, tilts her head, and lets it count. The old man gets his blanket and keeps every name. The witch says she will remember the story, which unsettles you more than it should.

failure.text: She hears the bargain for what it is and laughs. The old man, flustered, gives up his brother's name in a rush, and the blanket he wraps around himself smells of woodsmoke and loss.

choices.label: Ask what the names are for
choices.intent: Watch how she handles the jar, and ask her plainly what becomes of the names.
choices.risk: Some questions carry prices of their own.

success.text: The dead buried without names cannot find their way down to the deep water, she says, so she lends them borrowed ones. She is not cruel, only tired. She hands the old man a blanket for nothing, just once, and asks you to keep her secret.

failure.text: She seals the jar and stares at you until the line grows restless. Someone behind you mutters that you are slowing everyone down, and an elbow catches your ribs on your way out of the line.

choices.label: Shame her before the line
choices.intent: Tell the line loudly what they are giving up, and that no blanket is worth a brother.
choices.risk: Cold people may not thank you for the truth.

success.text: Half the line drifts away, holding on to their names. The other half stays; they are colder than they are sentimental. The witch does not argue; she only looks at you, and you know you will see her again.

failure.text: The line turns on you instead. A woman with two shivering children asks whether you have a blanket to give her, and when you don't, she spits at your feet. The witch carries on.

newCards.title: Loaves Against the Spring
newCards.flavor: A baker has built a clay oven in the hollow's warmest corner, and four round loaves are cooling on a slate beside it. She gives bread to anyone who will swear on the hollow's stone to repay her when the spring caravans come. You may be far from here by spring, and the echoes in this place are said to remember every oath.

choices.label: Swear and mean it
choices.intent: Swear the spring oath honestly, and plan to send the debt back by any road you can.
choices.risk: Spring is a long way off, and roads go wrong.

success.text: She hands you a loaf still warm in the middle. The oath goes into the stone and comes back to you in your own voice, very quietly, from somewhere behind you. It settles on your shoulders like a pack strap.

choices.label: Swear without meaning it
choices.intent: Speak the oath steadily, knowing you will be gone long before the caravans come.
choices.risk: The echoes here are said to catch a lying voice.

success.text: Your voice does not shake, and the echo comes back clean. She hands you a loaf and wishes you a safe road. You do not look at her as you leave, and you do not look back.

failure.text: The echo comes back wrong, cracked down the middle, and every head in the hollow turns. The baker takes the loaf back out of your hands without a word. Nobody here will trade with you now.

choices.label: Tell her you can't promise
choices.intent: Tell her plainly you may never come this way again, and walk on hungry.
choices.risk: Honesty won't fill your pack.

success.text: She nods and turns to the next in line. Nobody thanks you for being honest, but the echo of your refusal follows you out of the hollow, oddly clean, and you find you can carry it.

choices.label: Haul fuel for the oven
choices.intent: Offer to carry brush and dried dung up from the cave mouth in exchange for bread.
choices.risk: The climb is steep, and the storm has not broken.

success.text: Three trips up and down the slick passage, and the oven roars. The baker pays you a whole loaf with no oath attached, and tells the others in line that you worked for it.

failure.text: On the third trip you slip on wet stone and come down hard under the load, bruised from hip to shoulder. The baker winces for you, but bread is bread, and she has none to spare for half a load of brush.

newCards.title: Salt for the Burial
newCards.flavor: A miner kneels beside his wife's body on a bier of slate, pouring salt over her in a slow white line. By hollow custom the dead must be covered in salt or they wander the tunnels. That salt is everything his family has to trade for food, and his three children sit against the wall, watching it run out of the pouch.

choices.label: Feed the children quietly
choices.intent: Feed the children from your own pack so their father can finish the rite.
choices.risk: Your food won't stretch to the next hollow.

success.text: The children eat with their eyes on their father. He finishes the line of salt and never knows how close it came. When you leave, the eldest girl follows you to the passage and thanks you for both of them.

choices.label: Ask what she would want
choices.intent: Sit with him and ask what his wife would have wanted for the children.
choices.risk: Grief can turn on whoever is nearest.

success.text: He stops pouring. After a long time he lays only a pinch of salt on her eyes and ties the pouch shut. She would have smacked him for wasting it, he says, and laughs, and then cannot stop crying.

failure.text: He hears a stranger telling him how to bury his wife. He shoves you hard into the wall, bruising your shoulder, and pours out every grain, and the children watch the pouch go flat.

choices.label: Look for a salt seam
choices.intent: Search the hollow for a pale seam where rough salt can be scraped from the rock.
choices.risk: Old seams sit close to old collapses.

success.text: Behind the burial niche, a vein of grey salt runs through the wall. You and the miner scrape enough to cover her together, and his pouch goes back on his belt still full. He shows you the other seams his people know.

failure.text: You dig at the wrong pale streak until a shelf of shale slides across your arm. It is only gypsum, worthless, and you spend an hour picking grit out of the cut.

choices.label: Ask the hollow for pinches
choices.intent: Go round the sheltering families and ask each to spare one pinch for the burial.
choices.risk: Nobody down here has salt to spare.

success.text: Most say no. Then an old woman empties her twist of salt into your palm, and after that others follow, a pinch at a time. The dead woman is covered by the whole hollow, and her husband keeps his pouch.

failure.text: Blanket after blanket-door says no, some kindly and some not. By the time you come back, the pouch is empty and the white line is finished. You hand him the single pinch you were given.

newCards.title: Arrows in Children's Chalk
newCards.flavor: Someone's children have chalked arrows on every wall of the crossroads, little suns and stick dogs between them, pointing the way to the camp's water. Since the last tremor the tunnels have turned, and the arrows now point into a passage where you can hear water rising. Small fresh footprints lead into it, and a woman is calling two names down the wrong tunnel.

choices.label: Follow the small footprints
choices.intent: Follow the footprints into the flooding passage before the water closes it.
choices.risk: Rising water doesn't care who it catches.

success.text: Knee-deep, then waist-deep, then you find them on a ledge, clutching each other and a stub of chalk. You carry them out one at a time. Their mother hugs them, then you, then scolds all three of you for frightening her.

failure.text: The water knocks you down twice before you reach them. You get them out, but you swallow half the passage doing it and come out coughing and soaked, your pack lighter by everything that floated.

choices.label: Redraw the arrows
choices.intent: Scrub out the wrong arrows and chalk true ones before more children follow them.
choices.risk: The tunnels may turn again before the chalk is dry.

success.text: You work along the walls as fast as your hands will go, and by the time the mother comes back with two wet children, every arrow points true. Tracing the turned tunnels, you learn the road ahead has shifted too.

failure.text: You mix up two turns in the dark and chalk an arrow into a dead end yourself. A grandfather follows it and comes back bruised and furious, and you give him your supper by way of apology.

choices.label: Rouse the whole camp
choices.intent: Run to the camp and bring every grown pair of hands with rope and lamps.
choices.risk: Every minute spent fetching help, the water rises.

success.text: Twenty people come running with ropes and pot lids. They form a chain into the passage and pass the children out hand over hand. Nobody remembers afterward who raised the alarm, and you don't remind them.

failure.text: The camp is slow to wake and slower to believe you. By the time a rope chain forms, the mother has already dragged her children out herself, and she will not look at you.

newCards.title: The Bone Compass
newCards.flavor: At the crossroads, a crow-witch sits under a lantern with a compass carved from bone, its needle a single black quill. It points true even when the tunnels turn, she says, but only when it has been fed. A dish beside her holds a crust of bread, a smear of dried blood and a promise written on a curl of bark.

choices.label: Feed the compass bread
choices.intent: Lay a share of your food in her dish and ask the quill for the true way.
choices.risk: Food spent on a needle is food you won't eat.

success.text: The quill swings, shivers, and settles. She reads the way off it in a voice like a stranger's, and the tunnels ahead line up in an order you would never have chosen. Behind you, she breaks your bread for the refugee children.

choices.label: Feed the compass blood
choices.intent: Prick your hand over the dish and let the compass taste a stranger's blood.
choices.risk: Blood given to a witch's tool is not easily taken back.

success.text: The needle spins wildly, then points straight at you and stays there. The witch frowns, then laughs, and tells you the way anyway, and an old miners' road no tremor has ever moved. The road ahead is not the one you expected.

choices.label: Read the quill unfed
choices.intent: Wait until she turns to a customer, then watch which way the quill twitches on its own.
choices.risk: Witches notice who watches their tools.

success.text: The quill twitches toward the left-hand tunnel and away again, and you have it. You leave without paying, and the road ahead rearranges itself in your head. You are never quite sure whether you stole the way or she let you.

failure.text: She catches your eyes on the quill and turns the compass face down. When you take the left tunnel she calls after you, too pleasantly, that it floods at dusk. It does, and you come out soaked and short a meal.

choices.label: Offer a promise on bark
choices.intent: Write a promise to carry her message to the surface, and ask the compass to take it.
choices.risk: A promise to a witch is still a promise.

success.text: She reads your bark twice, folds it into her sleeve, and feeds it to the quill. The needle points, and she presses a small wax-sealed packet into your hand for someone at the far end of the depths. You have the way, and now a job.

failure.text: She reads your promise and tosses it back. Too vague, she says: you would keep it only if it suited you. The words sting more than they should, and the compass stays unfed.

newCards.title: The Surveyor's Tally Book
newCards.flavor: A territorial surveyor has come down to the crossroads with a lamp, a tally book and a mule loaded with grain. Every refugee he counts gets a ration. Every name he writes will also go to the counties they fled, and some of those counties want their debtors back. The side tunnels have gone silent, and he asks you which way the voices were coming from.

choices.label: Show him the camp
choices.intent: Lead him to the side tunnels, because the grain is real and the children are hungry.
choices.risk: Not every family down there can afford to be counted.

success.text: He counts sixty-one people and hands grain to every one of them. He also writes down the Mercer brothers, who ran from a county jail debt, and you see their faces when he does. He thanks you sincerely.

choices.label: Walk him in circles
choices.intent: Lead him through the turning passages until he tires and goes back up.
choices.risk: If he works it out, the camp gets no grain at all.

success.text: Two hours of turns, and he is tired enough to leave the grain at the crossroads for whoever needs it and climb out. The families come out after he is gone and press a handful of his grain on you. Nobody is counted, and nobody is sent back.

failure.text: He works it out at the third turn and looks at you with real disappointment. He writes your description in the back of his book, takes the grain back up with him, and the camp goes hungry.

choices.label: Let the families decide
choices.intent: Go to the camp first and tell them exactly what the surveyor offers and what he records.
choices.risk: Frightened people may scatter before anyone eats.

success.text: They argue in whispers for an hour. In the end forty come out to be counted and twenty stay hidden, and the counted carry grain back to the hidden. Nobody likes the arrangement, but everyone eats tonight.

failure.text: The word county goes through the camp like a cold draft, and half the families snatch up their bundles and flee deeper. You carry a sick child after the ones who ran, and come back exhausted.

choices.label: Trade him your own name
choices.intent: Offer him the one name the wardens want most, if he writes no others.
choices.risk: Your name in his book will travel faster than you.

success.text: His eyes widen; a face the wardens want is worth more to his superiors than sixty debtors. He writes you down, leaves the grain, and climbs out without looking at the side tunnels. The road ahead will have to bend around every town he reports to.

newCards.title: A Guide Who Never Came
newCards.flavor: A family of five has camped at the crossroads for three days, their fire built small to save fuel. The father shows you a guide's token, a brass disc stamped with a crow, bought with their mule. The guide was to lead them through to the far side. He has not come, and the mother asks you whether you know the way.

choices.label: Admit you are lost too
choices.intent: Tell them you are as lost down here as they are, and share what little you've seen.
choices.risk: The truth may take the last of their hope.

success.text: The mother nods as if she expected it. The father turns the brass disc over and over. You leave them your notes on the tunnels you have passed, and they thank you, and the fire is a little smaller when you go.

choices.label: Lead them anyway
choices.intent: Pick the likeliest tunnel and take them with you, trusting your reading of the stone.
choices.risk: Five people lost is worse than five people waiting.

success.text: You read the draft and the dust and choose right three times running. On the far side, the father presses the brass disc into your hand. You earned the mule, he says, which is a joke, because he has nothing else.

failure.text: The second turn is wrong, and so is the fourth. You get them back to their fire at last, everyone hungry, the youngest asleep on your back, and you share your food because you led them astray.

choices.label: Ask after the guide
choices.intent: Ask around the camp about the man who sold the token, and why he hasn't come.
choices.risk: Some people don't come back for reasons you won't like.

success.text: A woman at the next fire knows him. He was crushed in the tremor two days ago, and his apprentice has been too frightened to take on his jobs. You find the boy, thin as a rail; he agrees to try, and shows you the old miners' road his master used.

failure.text: Nobody wants to talk about the guide, and one man tells you flatly to stop asking. You learn nothing, and the family looks up at you with a hope you did not earn.

choices.label: Take them by the old road
choices.intent: Lead them by an old miners' road you learned, one the tremors never touch.
choices.risk: Old roads hold, but old roads are long.

success.text: The old road is long, dry, and exactly where you were told it would be. The family follows you out into grey daylight on the far side, and the way ahead of you is no longer the one you planned to walk.

failure.text: The old road is there, but half of it has fallen in. You get them through by crawling, and the climb over the rockfall costs you skin from both knees and most of a day's food.

newCards.title: Vows by the Last Lamp
newCards.flavor: In a side tunnel off the crossroads, two refugees want to marry before the camp's last lamp of oil burns out. They need a witness who is not kin. The bride's father stands across the lamp from them, refusing, because the groom comes from the county whose militia burned his farm, and half the camp is listening in the dark.

choices.label: Stand as their witness
choices.intent: Step into the lamplight beside the couple and say you will witness the vows.
choices.risk: The father will remember who stood against him.

success.text: You say the old words after them, and the lamp holds just long enough. The father walks out into the dark before the end. Afterward the couple give you a ribbon from the bride's hair, and the father will not share a fire with you.

choices.label: Talk to the father alone
choices.intent: Take the father aside and ask what he lost, before asking him to give anything.
choices.risk: His grief may outlast the oil in that lamp.

success.text: He talks about the farm, then about his wife who died in the smoke, then about how she married against her own father's wishes. He comes back to the lamp and stands at his daughter's shoulder. He does not smile, but he stays.

failure.text: He tells you to mind your own family, if you have one left. The lamp goes out before you get back, and the vows are finished in the dark, with nobody quite sure who heard them.

choices.label: Pour them your lamp oil
choices.intent: Pour the oil from your own lamp into theirs so there's time for everything.
choices.risk: You'll walk the next dark stretch half-blind.

success.text: The flame jumps up bright. There is time now for the father to speak, and after a long silence he does, one sentence of blessing that sounds dragged out of him. You walk the next stretch by the light of a dim wick.

choices.label: Ask the camp to speak
choices.intent: Ask the listeners in the dark whether this camp will carry old feuds underground.
choices.risk: Some of them lost farms too.

success.text: One by one, voices answer from the dark: an old drover, a widow, the woman who keeps the cookfire. They say it is time. The father hears his neighbors and lets his daughter go with a stiff nod.

failure.text: A man in the dark answers that the militia killed his son, and the camp splits along a line you had not seen. The wedding happens, but two families move their blankets to the far tunnel that night.

newCards.title: The Handcart and the Loom
newCards.flavor: A column of war refugees trudges the black road toward the camp's watchfires, and at the back of it an old weaver pushes a handcart with one wobbling wheel. Lashed on top is his dead wife's loom. The column's leader says they cannot wait for him any longer, and the ash is already thickening on the wind.

choices.label: Put your shoulder to the cart
choices.intent: Take the weight of the cart yourself so the old weaver can keep pace with the column.
choices.risk: The wheel could give out on the glass, and you with it.

success.text: You lean into the cart for miles, the axle shrieking, until the watchfires are close enough to read by. At the barricade the weaver unknots a cloth of flatbread from the loom's frame and makes you take half.

failure.text: The wheel splits on a ridge of glass and the cart pitches over, spilling the weaver's bundles across the road. You gather what you can while the column's lanterns shrink ahead, and you reach the camp bruised and long after dark.

choices.label: Ask him to leave the loom
choices.intent: Tell the weaver plainly that the loom will cost him the column, and maybe his life.
choices.risk: He may hear only that you want her left behind.

success.text: He is quiet a long time. Then he cuts one shuttle free, tucks it inside his coat, and leaves the loom standing by the road with her name scratched into the frame. He catches the column before the ash closes in.

failure.text: He hears only that you want her left behind, and turns his back on you. The column goes on without either of you, and by the time he lets you help, you have shared your food with him just to keep him walking.

choices.label: Carry the loom yourself
choices.intent: Unpack your own supplies onto the roadside to make room for the loom's frame and beams.
choices.risk: What you leave on the road, you will not see again.

success.text: You leave bread and a waterskin on a flat black stone for whoever comes next and strap the loom across your pack. The weaver says nothing all the way to the camp. At the gate he touches the frame and goes in without a word of thanks.

choices.label: Stay back with the weaver
choices.intent: You have walked away from someone before; this time you stay at the end of the column.
choices.risk: Alone at the rear, the ash and the cold find you first.

success.text: You let the column go and walk at the weaver's pace through the night while the cold settles deep into you. He talks about his wife the whole way. It does not undo the one you left behind, but you reach the camp together at dawn.

newCards.title: The Deserter's Cage
newCards.flavor: An iron cage hangs from a post beside the road, and inside it a young deserter squints against the heat rising off the stones. The key hangs on a nail just beyond his reach, under a painted board that forbids anyone to give him water. Dust from a mounted patrol is rising on the road behind you.

choices.label: Pass him your waterskin
choices.intent: Hold your waterskin up through the bars and let him drink as long as he needs.
choices.risk: The order on the board was written for people like you.

success.text: He drinks until he chokes, then drinks again, and thanks you through cracked lips. The patrol rider sees the wet bars as he passes and writes something down without stopping. You leave the deserter in the cage, already thirsty for tomorrow.

choices.label: Take the key from the nail
choices.intent: Wait for the patrol to pass, then lift the key and open the cage.
choices.risk: If the rider turns back, the cage has room for two.

success.text: You watch the rider's dust until it drops behind the ridge, then turn the key. The deserter runs bent double into the ash fields without looking back. You hang the key back on its nail, and the empty cage swings in the hot wind.

failure.text: The rider turns back sooner than you thought. The deserter runs and makes it; you don't. The rider's baton catches you across the ribs twice before he decides you are not worth the paperwork, and he rides off with your face in his memory.

choices.label: Ask him why he ran
choices.intent: Crouch in the cage's shadow and ask the deserter what made him leave his post.
choices.risk: He may be a liar with nothing left to lose.

success.text: He was ordered to burn a hamlet that hid no one, he says, and he could not. He tells you of a buried pilgrim track that skirts the next lava field, and the road ahead rearranges itself in your head. You leave him there because he asks you to.

failure.text: He spins a story about a sick mother that changes twice in the telling, then spits at you when you don't believe it. You walk on through the heat with nothing but his curses, and the sun leaves you light-headed and sick.

newCards.title: The Press-Gang at the Milestone
newCards.flavor: Beside a cracked milestone, a sergeant's press-gang is roping able bodies for the war beyond the ridge. They have taken a girl's older brother, the only one in her family strong enough to pull their cart. The sergeant shrugs at her crying: the camp wants a number of backs, and any back will do.

choices.label: Offer to take his place
choices.intent: Hold out your wrists for the rope so the brother can go back to his family's cart.
choices.risk: The sergeant's idea of a day's labor has no end.

success.text: They march you to the camp under a load of spear shafts and keep you hauling until others fill the sergeant's count. They let you go at midnight, wrung out and aching. The girl's family is long gone down the road, and no one is waiting to thank you.

choices.label: Read the conscription writ
choices.intent: Ask to see the sergeant's writ and look for any line that excuses the boy.
choices.risk: Sergeants dislike strangers who read better than they do.

success.text: The writ exempts the only able son of a family on the move, and you read the line aloud in front of the whole gang. The sergeant spits and cuts the rope. The brother takes up his cart without a word.

failure.text: The writ is plain and leaves no room, and the sergeant enjoys telling you so. When you argue, a gang member shoves you down onto the glass. The brother is led away, and the girl looks at you as if you had promised her something.

choices.label: Bribe the sergeant
choices.intent: Offer the sergeant food from your pack to look the other way for one boy.
choices.risk: He may take the food and the boy both.

success.text: The sergeant weighs the bread in his palm, looks at the boy, and decides one back is not worth arguing over. He waves the brother off with a curse. You walk on lighter, and the girl's family does not look back.

failure.text: He pockets the food and keeps the boy, and his men laugh. He does let the girl ride the supply wagon to the camp, so she will at least be near her brother. You walk the rest of the way with an emptier pack and nothing to show for it.

newCards.title: The Mule on the Glass
newCards.flavor: A peddler kneels beside her mule where it went down on a field of broken obsidian, its forelegs cut to ribbons. Everything she owns is in its panniers, and she cannot lift them. She asks you, quietly, to do the thing she cannot, and the mule's eyes roll white at every step you take.

choices.label: End the mule's suffering
choices.intent: Take the peddler's knife and do it quickly, while she holds the mule's head.
choices.risk: Some kindnesses stay with you longer than cruelties do.

success.text: It is quick, and she does not let go of the mule's head until it is over. Afterward she cuts you a share of the meat for the road and loads what she can onto her own back. Neither of you says much.

choices.label: Lead it along the ash
choices.intent: Search the road's edge for soft ash deep enough to walk the mule out of the glass.
choices.risk: The glass hides under the ash as often as not.

success.text: You find a shoulder of deep, soft ash and coax the mule onto it a step at a time. It limps, but it walks. By nightfall the peddler has reached the camp with her panniers, and she presses a twist of salted meat on you.

failure.text: The ash gives way over a buried edge of glass, and it opens your foot through your boot. The mule goes down again and does not get up. The peddler helps you bind the cut, and you limp on together in silence.

choices.label: Buy what she cannot carry
choices.intent: Offer her a little food for the goods she will have to leave behind anyway.
choices.risk: She will remember the price you named today.

success.text: She takes your offer because she has no other, and you shoulder a pannier of lamp oil, needles, and dried apricots. Before you are out of earshot you hear the mule cry out, then her knife, then nothing.

newCards.title: The Fork in the Black Glass
newCards.flavor: A fresh tongue of lava has split the road in two. The left fork swings wide around a burned hamlet, where someone on a roof keeps waving a white cloth. The right fork runs straight across a crust of new black glass, still ticking as it cools, and saves a day you may not have.

choices.label: Turn toward the white cloth
choices.intent: Take the long fork to the burned hamlet and find out who is waving.
choices.risk: A day lost on the road is a day's food gone.

success.text: An old couple has been waiting on the roof for three days, too frightened of the glass to come down. You share a meal with them, help them down, and point them toward the camp. They have nothing to give you, and the long fork costs you the afternoon.

choices.label: Cross the cooling crust
choices.intent: Step light and fast across the new glass to win back a day on the road.
choices.risk: New crust is thin, and what lies under it is not.

success.text: The glass is hot through your boots, and you keep walking anyway. From the high ground on the far side you see the road ahead has changed: old landmarks buried, a shorter way running toward the camp. Behind you, the white cloth is still waving.

failure.text: Halfway across, the crust cracks and your leg punches through into the heat beneath. You haul it out burned and limp the rest of the way, slower than the long fork would have been.

choices.label: Watch the cloth's rhythm
choices.intent: Study how the cloth is being waved before you commit to either fork.
choices.risk: Every hour you watch, the light fades a little more.

success.text: The cloth dips three times and then points, over and over: not a plea, a direction. It leads you along a ridge of old, hard glass to the hamlet, where a widow with a lookout's flag thanks you for understanding and gives you a handful of roasted beans.

failure.text: You watch too long. Dusk falls before you have made sense of the cloth, and you spend a cold night on the rocks between the forks, shivering, while the waving stops.

newCards.title: The Short Ration Line
newCards.flavor: At dawn the quartermaster ladles porridge from one black kettle into a line of refugees three times longer than the pot. The ledger on his table says there should be enough. A family at the very end of the line has already started to turn away, and a guard is shoving a man who came back for a second bowl.

choices.label: Give your bowl to the family
choices.intent: Step out of the line and hand your portion to the children at the end.
choices.risk: You will walk the last road on an empty stomach.

success.text: The children split the bowl three ways with their fingers. Their mother nods once and does not look at you again, as if your kindness were a debt she cannot afford. Your stomach complains all morning.

choices.label: Check the ledger against the pot
choices.intent: Count the line, read the ledger, and find where the missing porridge went.
choices.risk: Quartermasters have friends in the officers' tents.

success.text: The ledger counts sacks that never reached the kettle, and you find them stacked behind the officers' tent. You say so loudly enough for the whole line to hear. A second pot feeds everyone, and the quartermaster watches you with flat, patient hatred.

failure.text: The figures are smudged and the quartermaster is quicker than you. He calls you a thief in front of the line, and the guards hustle you out of the yard, taking a ration from your pack for the trouble.

choices.label: Ask who the bowl is for
choices.intent: Step between the guard and the man, and find out who the second bowl is for.
choices.risk: The guard has had a long night and a short temper.

success.text: It is for his wife, who is too fevered to stand in line. You walk the guard to her cot behind the wagons, and he stands there a long moment before telling the man to take the bowl. Nobody thanks you, but the shoving stops.

failure.text: The guard does not care who the bowl is for. He swings the ladle at the man and catches you instead, hard across the cheek, and the porridge spills into the ash for everyone to see.

choices.label: Set your bowl down first
choices.intent: You know how giving spreads; set your portion in the middle and let others follow.
choices.risk: If no one follows, you have simply given your breakfast away.

success.text: You set your bowl on an upturned crate and spoon the first share to the family at the end. Someone follows, then three more, until the line is feeding itself. When it is done, a neighbor hands you back a full bowl of your own.

failure.text: People look at the bowl, then at you, and keep their own portions close. You give yours to the family anyway. It is not enough for them, and you walk out of the yard hungry.

newCards.title: Two Cots, One Draught
newCards.flavor: In the infirmary tent, a surgeon holds up the camp's last vial of fever draught between two cots. On one lies a young sentry from the north wall; on the other, a captured raider who knows the only safe path across the ash flats. The commander wants the raider saved, the surgeon wants the sentry, and both of them turn to you.

choices.label: Give it to the sentry
choices.intent: Tell the surgeon to treat the sentry, whose mother is waiting on the north wall.
choices.risk: Without the raider, the camp loses its safe path.

success.text: The sentry's fever breaks by morning, and his mother presses a cloth of dried dates on you before she sits down to hold his hand. The raider dies before noon with the path still in his head, and the commander will not look at you.

choices.label: Give it to the raider
choices.intent: Tell the surgeon to treat the raider, because the path he knows could save more lives.
choices.risk: Some arithmetic is easier to do than to live with.

success.text: The raider lives and, weak and wary, draws the path across the ash flats on the commander's map; reading over her shoulder, you see the road ahead reorder itself. The sentry dies at dusk. His mother does not know you had a hand in it, and you do not tell her.

choices.label: Split the dose and nurse both
choices.intent: Halve the draught and sit up all night cooling both patients with wet cloths.
choices.risk: Half a dose might save neither of them.

success.text: You sponge two burning foreheads until your arms shake. By dawn both fevers have broken, barely, and the surgeon presses a parcel of broth biscuits into your hands as if paying for a trick she means to learn.

failure.text: Halfway through the night the raider's breathing changes, and nothing you do brings it back. The sentry lives. You come out into the grey morning exhausted, and the commander asks how it feels to have chosen after all.

choices.label: Open your own medicine pouch
choices.intent: Give the surgeon the fever herbs you have carried on the road so both can be treated.
choices.risk: Once those herbs are gone, you have nothing for yourself.

success.text: The surgeon steeps your herbs into a second dose, bitter and green, and both cots have their chance. By morning both patients are sitting up. Your pouch is empty now, and the surgeon has nothing to give you in return but a nod.

newCards.title: The Stockade at Dawn
newCards.flavor: At dawn the camp gathers at the stockade, where a raider in chains waits to hear whether he will hang. He says he rode with the raiders only because they fed his children, and half the crowd lost someone to his band. The commander asks for any stranger's testimony before the rope is thrown, and the crowd goes quiet when you step up.

choices.label: Argue for his life
choices.intent: Argue that a hanged man feeds no one, and he can work off the harm instead.
choices.risk: A grieving crowd may decide you are on the wrong side.

success.text: You talk until the commander raises her hand. The raider is sentenced to labor on the north wall in irons, and his children will eat from the camp kettle. Several in the crowd turn their backs on you, and one widow spits at your feet.

failure.text: The crowd hears a stranger defending a killer and surges. A thrown stone opens your brow, and the commander has guards walk you to the gate for your own safety. Behind you, the rope goes up.

choices.label: Tell what the road showed you
choices.intent: Tell the crowd honestly what raiders did on the road behind you, whatever it means for him.
choices.risk: Your words may be the last thing he hears.

success.text: You describe the burned farms you passed, plainly, adding nothing. The crowd listens in silence, and so does he. The rope goes up, and afterward the commander thanks you as though you had done her a favor.

choices.label: Question his story
choices.intent: Ask him the names and ages of his children, and watch how he answers.
choices.risk: The truth might be worse than the lie.

success.text: He answers without a pause, and a woman in the crowd says she has seen those children at the refugee fires. It does not save him from the irons, but it saves him from the rope, and at dusk his eldest finds you and shares a heel of bread from the refugee fires.

failure.text: His answers falter, and you cannot tell whether it is guilt or terror. Neither can the crowd. In the scuffle that follows an elbow catches your ribs, and you never learn whether he was lying.

choices.label: Tell of the foe you spared
choices.intent: Tell them about someone who wronged you, whom you spared, and what came of it.
choices.risk: Not everyone wants to hear that mercy can be chosen.

success.text: You tell it simply: someone hurt you, you let them go, and the world did not end. The raider is put to work instead of hanged, and as they lead him away he looks at you as though he owes you something he will have to carry.

failure.text: The crowd hears a story about someone else's wrong and decides it is not theirs to forgive. The rope goes up. Someone shoves you off the stockade steps on your way out, and you land hard on the packed ash.

newCards.title: The Rope Ladder at Night
newCards.flavor: After dark, a crowd of refugees presses against the camp's barred gate, begging to be let in. The gate sergeant will not lift the bar, because raiders have used refugees as cover before. A coiled rope ladder hangs on a peg beside the parapet, and below, a mother is holding a sleeping child up toward the torchlight.

choices.label: Lower the rope ladder
choices.intent: Drop the ladder over the parapet and pull up whoever can climb before the sergeant stops you.
choices.risk: Anyone can climb a ladder, raider or mother.

success.text: You haul up the mother and child, an old man, and a boy with burned hands before the sergeant's men drag you off the parapet and pin you hard to the boards. The sergeant writes your name in his book. The four you pulled up sleep by the cookfire tonight.

choices.label: Pick out the raiders below
choices.intent: Watch the crowd from the parapet for anyone armed, so the gate can open for the rest.
choices.risk: Misjudge one face, and the gate stays shut for everyone.

success.text: You spot three men at the back who stand too still, coats bulging at the hip. The sergeant's archers move them off, the bar lifts, and the rest stream in. Afterward the sergeant shares his supper with you by the watchfire.

failure.text: You point at a frightened farmer who turns out to be exactly that. The sergeant will not lift the bar for anyone after your mistake, and you throw your own ration over the wall to the mother as the torches burn down.

choices.label: Back the sergeant's rule
choices.intent: Tell the sergeant he is right to keep the gate barred until morning.
choices.risk: The night is long outside a barred gate.

success.text: The bar stays down. The sergeant, glad of an ally, shares a bowl of stew with you by the watchfire while the crying outside slowly stops. In the morning there are fewer people at the gate than there were at dusk.

newCards.title: The Dead Sentry's Boots
